intro.t: The shortest Gospel, probably the first written, moving fast to the cross.
b: Mark tells the story of Jesus at speed. ‘Immediately’ is one of his favourite words (the ESV Study Bible counts 41 uses), and there is no birth story and almost no long teaching. He shows Jesus acting with God’s authority over sickness, demons, nature, sin and death, and yet constantly misunderstood, even by his own disciples.

The Gospel turns on a question at its centre: ‘Who do you say I am?’ (8:29). Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ.’ From then on Jesus explains what kind of Christ he is: ‘the Son of Man must suffer’ (8:31), and he ‘did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many’ (10:45). Almost a third of the book covers his last week. The first human being in Mark to call Jesus ‘the Son of God’ is a Roman centurion watching him die (15:39). The point is to follow him: the ESV Study Bible sums up Mark’s purpose as ‘to present and defend Jesus’ universal call to discipleship’.

What the early church said. The Gospel does not name its author, but every early witness gives the same answer. Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor writing early in the 2nd century and quoted by Eusebius, passed on what ‘the elder’ had told him: ‘Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.’ Irenaeus (about AD 180) writes of Peter and Paul: ‘After their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, did also hand down to us in writing what had been preached by Peter.’ The anti-Marcionite prologue adds that Mark wrote in Italy.

Where scholars stand. Every surviving manuscript carries the title ‘According to Mark’; Martin Hengel and Richard Bauckham argue that the titles go back to the first copies. The Lexham Bible Dictionary estimates that about 60 percent of scholars accept that John Mark wrote it; the rest regard the author as unknown, usually because they doubt Papias.

The case for Mark. If the church had been inventing an author, it would hardly have chosen Mark. He was not an apostle. He was the young man who abandoned Paul and Barnabas on their first journey (Acts 13:13; 15:37–39), though later Paul called him ‘useful to me for the ministry’ (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter calls him ‘my son Mark’ in a letter from ‘Babylon’, probably Rome (1 Peter 5:13). The Gospel itself fits Papias’s description: vivid, eyewitness-like detail, Peter prominent and his failures told plainly, and an outline that matches Peter’s preaching in Acts 10:36–43, from John’s baptism to the resurrection.

b: Rome, for Gentile believers (Widely accepted). Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4), translates Aramaic words (5:41; 7:34; 15:34), and uses Latin terms written in Greek letters, such as legion, denarius and praetorium. It mentions Rufus (15:21), perhaps the Rufus greeted in Romans 16:13. Christians in Rome suffered terribly under Nero after the fire of AD 64; Tacitus and 1 Clement describe it. A Gospel that spends so much time on suffering, betrayal and faithfulness under trial would speak directly to them. Some scholars suggest Syria or Galilee instead.

Date (Debated). Those who accept the tradition date it shortly after Peter’s death, about AD 65–70. Most think it was written before the temple was destroyed in AD 70, since Mark does not describe the event. A few date it soon after 70, reading 13:14 as a reference to it. Others date it earlier still, in the mid- to late 50s. Acts ends with Paul in prison in Rome about AD 62, which suggests it was finished then; Luke came before Acts, and Luke used Mark (J. A. T. Robinson; the ESV Study Bible thinks this the most likely date, while allowing the mid-60s). Clement of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius (Church History 2.15; 6.14), says Mark wrote while Peter was alive and that Peter approved the book. Irenaeus’s ‘departure’ of Peter and Paul may mean their leaving Rome rather than their deaths (ESV Study Bible).

hist.t: Matthew, Mark and Luke: who used whom? (the ‘Synoptic problem’)
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell many of the same stories, often in the same order and with the same wording; they are called the ‘Synoptic’ Gospels (Greek: ‘seen together’). Of Mark’s 661 verses, about 606 have a parallel in Matthew and about 380 in Luke; only some 31 verses of Mark have no parallel in either.

Mark first (Widely accepted). Since the 19th century most scholars have concluded that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, smoothing its rough Greek and adding their own material. The material Matthew and Luke share but Mark lacks (about 200–250 verses, mostly sayings of Jesus) is usually explained by a lost collection of sayings called ‘Q’ (from German Quelle, ‘source’). Some suggest Papias’s remark that Matthew compiled ‘the oracles’ refers to something like it.

Other views (Debated). Augustine thought Mark had abridged Matthew, and many Catholic scholars long defended Matthew’s priority; a minority still argue that Matthew came first, or that Luke used Matthew directly with no need for Q. No copy of Q has ever been found.

None of these theories requires that the Gospel writers were careless or untrustworthy. Luke openly says he used earlier accounts and eyewitness testimony (Luke 1:1–4). Using written sources was normal and responsible history-writing.

b: The Jewish historian Josephus (about AD 37–100) mentions Jesus twice. In Antiquities 20.200 he records the stoning of ‘the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James’. Almost all scholars accept this passage as genuine.

In Antiquities 18.63–64 our copies call Jesus ‘a wise man’ and ‘a doer of wonderful works’, and say Pilate condemned him to the cross. But they also contain phrases a non-Christian Jew is unlikely to have written (for example ‘He was the Christ’). Many scholars therefore think Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral passage about Jesus and that Christian copyists later added to it. Others think the whole passage is a later insertion; a few defend it as it stands. Either way, the passage on James shows that Josephus knew of Jesus.

1.h: The first line is the thesis
1.t: Mark does not open with a genealogy or a nativity but with a claim. “Beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis: something is starting here on that scale. “Gospel” was not yet a religious word — in the Roman world it announced an imperial victory or the birth of an emperor. To attach it to an executed Galilean is a political provocation as much as a theological one. Note the footnote: some early manuscripts lack “the Son of God”, though the phrase reappears at the centre and the climax of the book regardless.

1.h: All three persons at the Jordan
1.t: The Son is baptised, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The Trinity is not a doctrine developed centuries later and read backwards into the text; it is simply what is happening in this scene. The Father’s words splice Psalm 2:7, spoken to the messianic king, with Isaiah 42:1, spoken to the suffering Servant. Both identities are assigned before Jesus has done anything, and the tension between them drives the rest of the Gospel.

Mark gives the temptation two verses where Matthew and Luke give forty. The verb is violent — the Spirit throws him out into the wilderness. Israel spent forty years in the wilderness and failed; Jesus spends forty days and does not. The wild animals are Mark’s detail alone, and may hint at Eden restored.

Nothing is said about why they follow. Mark is not interested in their psychology but in his authority: he speaks, and men leave their livelihood mid-shift. Zebedee is left in the boat with the hired men, which tells you this was a business of some size. Following costs something real from the first sentence.

The crowd’s reaction is that he teaches with authority, “not as the scribes”. A scribe’s authority was derivative — he cited those before him. Jesus cites nobody. The demon, notably, is the first character in the Gospel to identify him correctly, and is immediately silenced. Throughout Mark the supernatural realm knows exactly who he is while the human characters do not.

Under the law, touching a leper made you unclean. Jesus touches him and the man is cleansed instead. The direction of contagion reverses. This is a small picture of the whole gospel: holiness that goes out and absorbs rather than holiness that withdraws and protects itself.

2.t: The scribes’ reasoning is impeccable: only God forgives sins, therefore this is blasphemy. Their logic is right and their conclusion is wrong, and the only way out is the one they will not take. Jesus does not soften the claim; he proves it with something visible. “Son of Man” here is not a modest self-description — it is drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where a human figure approaches the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion.

Levi collected tax for Rome from his own people, which made him a collaborator as well as a thief. Table fellowship in this culture signalled acceptance, which is precisely why the objection is raised. Jesus’ reply is not that these people are fine as they are — he calls them sick and himself the doctor. Both halves of that matter.

2.h: Not a patch on the old
2.t: The new wine imagery is often softened into a general point about change. Its actual force is sharper: what Jesus brings cannot be contained inside the existing structures of Second Temple religion. Something is being replaced, not renovated.

3.h: The alliance that should not exist
3.t: Pharisees were religious separatists; Herodians were political collaborators with Rome. They agreed on almost nothing except, now, this. Mark places the decision to kill Jesus in chapter three of sixteen — the outcome is fixed before a third of the book has passed, and everything after moves toward it.

The number is the point. Twelve tribes, twelve apostles: Jesus is constituting a renewed Israel around himself. Judas is named in the list from the beginning, with his end already attached, which Mark does without comment.

This passage has caused more unnecessary fear than almost any other. What Jesus condemns is the settled, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit’s work to Satan — looking at undeniable good and calling it evil in order to avoid its implications. It is a hardened position, not a moment of doubt or a blasphemous thought that intruded. The pastoral point follows logically: anyone anxious about having committed it has demonstrated by that anxiety that they have not. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

Mark sandwiches the Beelzebul controversy inside the story of Jesus’ family coming to seize him because they think he is out of his mind. The structure is intentional. Both his relatives and the religious authorities conclude something is wrong with him; the difference is only in what they blame.

4.t: The parable is not primarily about identifying which soil you are. It is an explanation of why the ministry is producing such mixed results, and a promise that despite the waste the harvest will be absurdly large. Thirty, sixty and a hundredfold were extraordinary yields in first-century Palestine, where sevenfold was a good year.

4.h: The hardest verses in the chapter
4.t: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 to explain that parables both reveal and conceal. This sits uncomfortably with modern assumptions, and it should. The point is that hearing is not a neutral capacity everyone possesses and some choose to use; genuine understanding is given. Those already resisting find that the parables harden the resistance. This is why the disciples’ access to explanation is a gift rather than a reward — they understand no better than anyone else, as the next four chapters repeatedly show. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something God does and nobody else — Psalm 107:29 is the closest parallel and the disciples would have known it. Their terror after the calm is greater than their terror during the storm, and rightly so. The question they ask is Mark’s question, and he will not answer it plainly until chapter 8.

5.t: A Roman legion was roughly six thousand men, and the name is unlikely to be accidental in a Gospel written for readers under Roman power. The setting is Gentile territory — hence the pigs — and the healed man becomes the first person commissioned to tell rather than to keep silent. Outside Israel, the misunderstanding that the secret protects against does not apply.

Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus’s story, and the two are linked by the number twelve — she has bled for twelve years, the girl is twelve years old. Both are ritually unclean situations; both are reversed by touch. Jairus has to stand and wait while his daughter dies, which is Mark’s honest acknowledgement that delay is part of the experience even when the outcome is good.
Mark preserves the actual words — talitha koum — and then translates them. He does this several times. It is the kind of detail that survives when a story comes from someone who was in the room.

6.t: Mark says plainly that Jesus could do no miracle there beyond a few healings, and that he marvelled at their unbelief. This is not a statement about a shortage of divine power; it is a statement about the nature of what he came to do. Miracles in Mark are never displays for their own sake — they meet faith, and where there is none they have nothing to meet.

The execution of John is the single passage in Mark where Jesus does not appear, and it is told in unusual detail. Its placement, between the sending of the Twelve and their return, is a warning shot: this is what happens to those who speak for God to people in power. Mark’s first readers, under Nero, would not have missed it.

“Sheep without a shepherd” is a quotation, not a sentiment — it comes from Numbers 27:17 and is picked up in Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s leaders and promises to shepherd the flock himself. Sitting them down on green grass points at Psalm 23. Mark is telling you who is doing the feeding.

6.h: He meant to pass by them
6.t: An odd detail until you notice where it comes from. In Exodus 33 and 1 Kings 19, God “passes by” Moses and Elijah — it is the technical language of a divine appearance. Combined with the words rendered “It is I”, which in Greek are simply “I am”, this is a theophany on the water. Mark closes by noting the disciples’ hearts were hardened, using the same word he applies to the Pharisees.

7.t: The specific abuse is declaring property dedicated to the temple so that it becomes unavailable to support ageing parents, while the declarer retains its use. Jesus’ charge is not that tradition is worthless but that this tradition is being used to cancel a commandment. The principle generalises uncomfortably well.

The clause declaring all foods clean is Mark’s editorial note, not part of Jesus’ speech. It is a remarkable thing for a first-century Jewish writer to say, and it indicates how far the implications had been worked out by the time he wrote. The food laws that separated Israel from the nations are over.

7.h: The only person who wins an argument
7.t: Jesus’ words to the Syrophoenician woman are deliberately hard, and attempts to soften them usually make the passage worse. She does not dispute the priority he states — she accepts it and presses for the overflow. She is the only character in the Gospels who takes Jesus’ own image and turns it, and he commends her for exactly that. Immediately afterwards he feeds a Gentile crowd.

8.t: Two feedings have happened and the disciples worry about bread. Jesus’ questions here — do you have eyes and fail to see, ears and fail to hear — apply to the disciples the same language chapter 4 applied to outsiders. The gap between them and the crowd is smaller than they think.

The only miracle in the Gospels that takes two attempts, and it is placed here deliberately. The man first sees people looking like walking trees, then sees clearly. In the very next scene Peter identifies Jesus correctly and then immediately misunderstands what it means. The healing is a deliberate commentary on the confession that follows.

Caesarea Philippi was a centre of pagan worship, which makes it a pointed place to ask the question. Peter’s answer is right, and Jesus orders silence. This is the midpoint of the book; from here the geography turns toward Jerusalem and the subject turns to the cross.

Peter is rebuked in the strongest terms in the Gospel, moments after being right. The rebuke is not for doubting that Jesus is Messiah but for assuming he knows what a Messiah does. Note the word “must” in the prediction — the cross is not a tragic accident that befalls the plan; it is the plan.

9.t: Moses and Elijah represent the law and the prophets; their presence and then their disappearance, leaving Jesus alone, is the point of the scene. The Father’s command echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen. Peter’s instinct to build shelters is an attempt to make a permanent arrangement of a moment that was never meant to be one.

9.h: The most honest prayer in the Bible
9.t: “I believe; help my unbelief” is a contradiction, and it is answered anyway. It is worth noticing what Jesus does not do: he does not tell the man to come back when he is more certain. Faith that is mixed with doubt is still faith, and it is still enough. Most Christians will pray this sentence at some point, and they are in good company.

The second passion prediction is followed immediately by the disciples debating which of them is greatest. Mark reports this without editorial comment, which is its own comment. Jesus’ answer places a child — a person of no status whatever in that society — at the centre of the room.

10.t: Asked to take a side in a rabbinic dispute about grounds for divorce, Jesus goes past the Mosaic concession to Genesis. The permission existed, he says, because of hardness of heart — a regulation of failure rather than a statement of intent. He treats the creation account as normative and as historical, which is worth noting on its own.

10.h: Jesus looked at him and loved him
10.t: Mark alone records the look and the love, which changes the tone of everything that follows. The demand is not a general requirement laid on all disciples but a diagnosis of this man’s particular idol, aimed precisely. The disciples’ astonishment reflects an assumption that wealth signalled God’s favour. Jesus’ answer — that it is impossible for anyone, and possible only with God — is as clear a statement of salvation by grace as the Gospels contain.

The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. “Ransom” is a marketplace and slave-market word: a price paid to secure release. “For many” echoes Isaiah 53:11–12 and the Servant who bears the sins of many. Every major strand of the New Testament’s understanding of the cross is already present in this one sentence, spoken by Jesus about himself.

Bartimaeus is the only person healed in Mark whose name is recorded. He addresses Jesus as Son of David — a messianic title — and is not silenced, because Jerusalem is now in view. Mark ends the account by saying he followed Jesus on the road, and the road leads directly to the cross. He is the model disciple, and he is a blind beggar.

11.t: The arrangements are too specific to be spontaneous. Jesus is staging Zechariah 9:9 — a king coming humble and riding on a donkey, the animal of peace rather than the warhorse. The crowd’s shout comes from Psalm 118. They are expecting a different kind of king from the one they have.

11.h: The fig tree and the temple
11.t: Mark splits the fig tree around the temple cleansing, which is the clearest example of his sandwiching technique. The tree is in leaf but bears nothing; the temple is in operation but produces nothing. One interprets the other. The quotation about a house of prayer for all nations comes from Isaiah 56:7, and the trading was taking place in the only court Gentiles were permitted to enter.

Jesus' promises about prayer are real and bold, but they sit inside the rest of Scripture, where Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass and was not spared, and Paul's thorn was not removed. The historic Christian understanding is that God always hears and always answers in love, sometimes by giving what we ask, sometimes by giving something better, and sometimes by giving himself in the waiting. Unanswered prayer is not usually evidence of weak faith; it is one of the ordinary experiences of every believer in Scripture. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

12.t: The vineyard is Isaiah 5, and the audience recognised it immediately — Mark tells us they knew the parable was about them. The escalation from servants to the beloved son is the whole history of Israel’s prophets, and Jesus places himself at the end of it in a category of his own.

The trap is real: say yes and lose the crowd, say no and face Rome. Jesus’ answer is not a tidy separation of religion and politics. The coin bears Caesar’s image so return it to him — and you bear God’s image, so the question of what is owed to God answers itself and is not a small one.

Usually read as a lesson in generosity, and it is. But notice its placement, directly after Jesus condemns scribes who devour widows’ houses and immediately before he predicts the temple’s destruction. The woman gives everything to an institution that is about to fall and that has been exploiting people like her. The admiration and the lament are held together.

13.t: Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world and some of its foundation stones weighed over fifty tonnes. The prediction was literally fulfilled in AD 70, within the lifetime of many who heard it.

The discourse moves between the fall of Jerusalem and the final return, and interpreters divide over where the line falls. The most defensible reading takes the detailed warnings about Judea as concerning AD 70, and the cosmic language from verse 24 as concerning the end. Whatever the division, the repeated instruction is not to calculate but to stay awake — and Jesus states plainly that the day is not known even to the Son. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

14.h: She has done what she could
14.t: The perfume was worth close to a year’s wages. The objection about the poor is reasonable, and Jesus does not dismiss it so much as subordinate it to the moment. Sandwiched between Judas’s betrayal arrangements on either side, the contrast is stark: one person pours out everything, another sells him for silver.

“This is my body” is said while his body is visibly present, which should govern how literally the words are taken. The covenant language comes from Exodus 24 and Jeremiah 31. Christians have divided for centuries over what happens at the table; what is not in dispute is that his death is being interpreted, by him, in advance, as a sacrifice that establishes a covenant.

Mark preserves the Aramaic word for Father, the ordinary family word. The prayer asks for the cup to pass and then submits, and both halves are recorded. This is the clearest window in the Gospels into the genuine humanity of Jesus — not a performance of distress but distress. That he asks and is not spared says something important about what unanswered prayer can mean.

Asked directly whether he is the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One, Jesus answers with two words that in Greek are simply “I am”, and then combines Daniel 7 with Psalm 110. He claims divine identity, enthronement and the role of coming judge in one sentence. The high priest’s reaction shows the claim was understood exactly as intended.

If this Gospel carries Peter’s testimony, then the most humiliating account of Peter in the New Testament comes from Peter. Mark records no rehabilitation scene; the only forward-looking word is the message at the tomb that names Peter specifically.

15.t: Jesus quotes the opening line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic. Two things are true at once and both matter. He is genuinely bearing abandonment, and he is reaching for Scripture to say so — and Psalm 22, which begins in that darkness, ends in vindication and worldwide worship. The quotation is not despair with no floor under it.
The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from everything else and enforced the distance between God and people. Mark specifies the direction of the tear. This is not something achieved from below.

Mark’s whole argument lands here. The first human being in the Gospel to confess Jesus as Son of God is a Roman officer who has just supervised his execution, and what convinces him is not a miracle but the manner of the death. This closes the frame opened in 1:1 — and the fact that it is a Gentile who sees it first would not have been lost on Mark’s readers in Rome.

16.h: An ending that does not feel like one
16.t: The women are told that he is risen and that the disciples — and Peter by name — will see him. Then they flee and say nothing, and the Greek text ends on a conjunction, mid-breath. Many readers have found this unsatisfying; it may be exactly the point. The one group in the Gospel who obey and speak are the readers, and Mark has left the last move to them.

Most modern Bibles mark this passage off, and the BSB is no exception. The two earliest and most reliable complete manuscripts of Mark end at verse 8, as do several early translations and patristic witnesses; the longer ending uses vocabulary and style found nowhere else in Mark. Some manuscripts carry a shorter alternative ending instead. None of this is hidden or recent — translators flag it precisely because the evidence is public, and no Christian doctrine depends on these verses. It is a good example of textual criticism working as it should.

1.h: The Mission of John the Baptist
1.ctx: Mark’s is the shortest Gospel, and the book does not name its author. Papias, an early church writer quoted by the historian Eusebius, passed on what ‘the presbyter’ said: that Mark, ‘having become the interpreter of Peter’, wrote down what he remembered of Peter’s teaching; many scholars, including Donald English, identify him with John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul (Acts 12:12; 1 Peter 5:13). English thinks Rome the likeliest destination. Mark has no birth story: he starts with John the Baptist preaching in the wilderness near the Jordan.
1.mean: Mark’s first line works like a title for the whole book: ‘This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.’ The word ‘gospel’ means ‘good news’. In Mark’s world it was used for big public announcements, such as the birth of an emperor (English). Mark is announcing news that changes everything, and the news is a person. Jesus is the one who brings the good news, and he is the good news. As Donald English puts it, ‘The messenger is also the message.’ Where does the good news begin? Not in Bethlehem, but with a voice in the wilderness. Mark quotes two prophets about a messenger sent ahead to get the road ready for the Lord. A king’s visit needed the road levelled; God’s coming needs hearts made ready. That messenger is John. John looks like Elijah, the fiery prophet of old, with his camel-hair cloak and leather belt, and he lives on wild food. He calls people to ‘a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins’. Repentance means turning round: turning away from sin and back to God. Washing with water was a familiar religious picture of being made clean, but John asks God’s own people to be washed, as if they too were outsiders who needed a fresh start. Crowds pour out of Jerusalem and the Judean countryside, confessing their sins. Yet John points away from himself. Someone far greater is coming, so great that John is not fit to do a slave’s job of untying his sandals. John can only wash people with water. The one coming will baptize them ‘with the Holy Spirit’. Mark wants you to see that the whole Old Testament has been leaning forward to this moment.
1.big: Mark opens with good news about Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and with John, the promised messenger, who prepares the way by calling people to turn back to God and pointing to the greater one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.

vv.h: This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God
b: ‘Beginning’ may echo the first words of Genesis (‘In the beginning’): God is making a fresh start (English). Calvin read the verse more narrowly: Mark rightly starts the gospel with John’s preaching, because the old order of the Law and the Prophets ran until John, so ‘the beginning of the Gospel, strictly speaking, took place when John began to preach’. Wesley agreed: the beginning ‘is in the account of John the Baptist, contained in the first paragraph; the Gospel itself in the rest of the book.’

‘Jesus’ is his personal name; ‘Christ’ is a title, the Greek form of ‘Messiah’, the anointed king Israel was waiting for. ‘Son of God’ will run through the whole book, from the Father’s voice at the baptism (1:11) to the Roman centurion at the cross (15:39). Some early manuscripts lack the words ‘the Son of God’ here; see Where readings differ. The ESV Study Bible notes that in the Old Testament ‘good news’ is tied to God keeping his promises (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7; Nahum 1:15).

vv.h: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet
b: The first quotation comes mainly from Malachi: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me’ (Malachi 3:1), with an echo of Exodus 23:20, where God sends an angel ahead of Israel. The second is Isaiah: ‘Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness’ (Isaiah 40:3). Mark names only Isaiah. Writers of the time often gathered texts on one theme under the name of the best-known prophet (English), and Isaiah 40 is the passage about God coming to comfort and rescue his people. Cooper suggests Mark named Isaiah ‘probably because Isaiah emphasized the servanthood and salvation of the Messiah’. Some manuscripts (the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus) read ‘in the prophets’ instead, as the BSB footnote records, possibly because copyists found the single name awkward.

Notice a quiet but huge change. In Malachi God speaks of the way ‘before Me’; in Mark it becomes ‘ahead of You’, and Isaiah’s highway ‘for our God’ becomes paths ‘for Him’. Words about the LORD himself are applied to Jesus (English).

vv.h: preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins
b: Jews knew ritual washings, and non-Jews who joined Israel were baptized. What startled people was John asking Jews to be baptized, as though belonging to Israel was not enough by itself (English; Cooper). Repentance is more than feeling sorry. The Old Testament idea behind it is ‘turning back’ to God, a change of direction for the whole life (English). Wesley summed up John’s work as ‘preaching repentance, and baptizing as a sign and means of it.’ The ESV Study Bible sees a new exodus here: Israel comes out into the wilderness and, so to speak, enters the Jordan again, as when it first entered the promised land (Joshua 3–4), to receive what God has promised.

vv.h: John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist
b: This is the dress of Elijah, ‘a hairy man … with a leather belt around his waist’ (2 Kings 1:8). Malachi had promised, ‘I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD’ (Malachi 4:5). Mark will later make the link plain (9:11–13). Locusts and wild honey were the food of the wilderness: John lives simply, outside the comforts and power of Jerusalem.

vv.h: the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie
b: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. John says he is not worthy even of that. Wesley: ‘to do him the very meanest service.’ John, the greatest prophet of his day, makes himself small so that Jesus may be seen.

vv.h: I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit
b: The main contrast is between two persons, John and Jesus, more than between two baptisms (English). The prophets had promised that God would wash his people and put his Spirit within them: ‘I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean’ (Ezekiel 36:25) and ‘I will put My Spirit within you’ (Ezekiel 36:27). Matthew and Luke add ‘and with fire’; Mark, who leaves out John’s warnings of judgment, has only the Spirit. Jesus himself links John’s words to the coming of the Spirit after his resurrection (Acts 1:5). How that promise applies to Christians today is discussed in Where readings differ.

1.diff:
‘The Son of God’ in verse 1. Some early manuscripts lack these words. The BSB prints them, following the main critical edition (ECM) and the Byzantine text; its footnote records that two other critical editions (SBL and Westcott–Hort) leave them out. Those who leave them out argue that scribes were more likely to add a title of honour than to drop one. Those who keep them, including Donald English, reply that a short phrase is easily lost in copying, that the support for it is strong, and that ‘Son of God’ is Mark’s great theme (1:11; 3:11; 9:7; 15:39). Either way, Mark plainly teaches that Jesus is the Son of God.

Baptism with the Holy Spirit today. Pentecostals such as the Assemblies of God teach that ‘the baptism in the Holy Spirit’ is an experience that all believers should seek, that it is ‘distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth’, and that ‘This was the normal experience of all in the early Christian Church’, citing Acts 8:12–17 and 10:44–46 among other passages (Statement of Fundamental Truths, 7). Others, including Calvin and Donald English, read John’s promise as fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2) and given to every Christian at conversion; Paul says that ‘if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ’ (Romans 8:9). English put it this way: ‘All who know Christ are already baptized in the Spirit.’ English and the Assemblies of God both want Christians to live in the Spirit’s fullness.

b: Malachi ends the Old Testament prophets by promising a messenger, Elijah, before the Lord comes to his temple (Malachi 3:1; 4:5). Mark opens by saying: he has come. Isaiah 40 begins, ‘Comfort, comfort My people’, and announces that God himself is coming to rescue his people, like a shepherd gathering lambs (Isaiah 40:1–11). Mark tells you that when Jesus comes, God has come.

Ezekiel 36 promised a cleansing with water and the gift of God’s Spirit, so that God’s people would at last walk in his ways. John’s water baptism pictures the first half; Jesus brings the second. Joel promised the Spirit poured out ‘on all people’ (Joel 2:28), and Peter said this happened at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–18).

l.t: ‘I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.’
A voice calling: prepare the way for the LORD.
God sends an angel ahead of Israel along the way.
Elijah: a hairy man with a leather belt.
Clean water, a new heart and God’s Spirit within.
Matthew’s account, with John’s warnings to the Pharisees and Sadducees.
Luke’s account, with John’s practical advice to the crowds.
John the Baptist: ‘I am not the Christ.’
Jesus: you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.

qs: What does John wear, eat and say, and what do these details tell you about him?
Why do you think Mark begins the good news with John in the wilderness rather than with Jesus’ birth?
John made himself small so that Jesus could be seen. Where might you need to do the same?

b: The Jewish historian Josephus calls him ‘John, that was called the Baptist’ and ‘a good man’ who urged the Jews to practise righteousness and piety and to come to baptism. He records that Herod Antipas, fearing that John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a rebellion, had him imprisoned and executed at the fortress of Machaerus (compare Mark 6:14–29). Josephus differs from the Gospels in two ways: he says John’s washing was acceptable to God not as a means of putting away some sins but ‘for the purification of the body’, the soul having been ‘thoroughly purified beforehand by righteousness’, and he gives Herod’s motive as fear of revolt, where Mark gives John’s rebuke over Herodias. The two reasons are not exclusive.

1.ctx: Jesus comes south from Nazareth, an obscure village in Galilee never mentioned in the Old Testament, to the Jordan, where John is baptizing. Mark tells the scene in three verses. Matthew adds John’s protest (Matthew 3:14–15) and John’s Gospel tells how John recognised Jesus (John 1:29–34).
1.mean: Jesus arrives without fanfare. He comes from Nazareth, a village nobody expected anything from, and he joins the queue of people being baptized by John. That is surprising. John’s baptism was for people turning from their sins, and the Gospels teach that Jesus had no sins to turn from (Hebrews 4:15). Why, then, is he baptized? Christians have given several answers that fit together. Jesus stands with the people he came to save, in the very place where they admit their need. He obeys his Father’s will. And he starts down a road that will end at the cross, which he later calls a ‘baptism’ (10:38). As Jesus comes up out of the water, Mark says he saw the heavens ‘breaking open’, as if torn apart. Isaiah had prayed, ‘If only You would rend the heavens and come down’ (Isaiah 64:1). Now God is answering that prayer. The Spirit comes down on Jesus ‘like a dove’. The Spirit hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2); now he rests on Jesus at the start of a new creation. Then the Father speaks: ‘You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.’ These words echo two Old Testament passages. Psalm 2 speaks of God’s anointed King: ‘You are My Son.’ Isaiah 42 speaks of God’s Servant, on whom God puts his Spirit and in whom he delights. Jesus is both: the royal Son and the humble Servant who will suffer. Here, at the very start of Mark, you meet the Father who speaks, the Son who is loved, and the Spirit who comes down. This is the one God the church confesses as Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (English speaks of the passage’s ‘natural trinitarianism’). The Father’s love for the Son does not begin here; it is spoken out loud here, as Jesus begins his work.
1.big: At his baptism Jesus stands with sinners, the heavens are torn open, the Spirit comes down on him, and the Father declares him his beloved Son, both royal King and humble Servant.

vv.h: Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John
b: English calls the baptism ‘a sure sign of the authenticity of the event’: the early church would hardly invent a story of the sinless Son of God receiving a baptism of repentance. Calvin gave two reasons for it: the general reason ‘that he might render full obedience to the Father’, and the special reason ‘that he might consecrate baptism in his own body, that we might have it in common with him’. Cooper adds that Jesus identified himself with sinful people (2 Corinthians 5:21).

vv.h: He saw the heavens breaking open
b: Mark’s verb is stronger than Matthew’s and Luke’s ‘opened’: English renders it ‘torn open’. Calvin thought Mark’s words describe a real opening of the visible sky, and English notes that tearing open the heavens was a Jewish way of introducing a revelation from God (Isaiah 64:1; Ezekiel 1:1). At the end of the Gospel the temple veil is ‘torn in two’ as Jesus dies (15:38): God breaks in at the start of Jesus’ ministry and at its end.

vv.h: the Spirit descending on Him like a dove
b: In Mark, Jesus sees this, and the voice speaks to him (‘You are…’). John’s Gospel says John the Baptist saw it too (John 1:32–34). English concludes that the vision was both a personal assurance to Jesus and a public sign. English links the dove with the Spirit over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). The Spirit is anointing Jesus for his work; ‘Messiah’ means ‘anointed one’.

vv.h: You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased
b: Psalm 2:7: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father’, words to God’s chosen King. Isaiah 42:1: ‘Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him.’ English stresses that ‘There is no sense of God ‘adopting’ Jesus as son at the baptism’: the Father declares who Jesus already is.

The voice joins two figures the Old Testament held side by side: the King of Psalm 2 who will rule the nations, and the Servant of Isaiah 42–53 who will suffer for his people. Much of Mark’s story will show that Jesus is King precisely by being the suffering Servant (10:45).

Christians are baptized ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19), and the same three are present here. Calvin saw Jesus consecrating baptism ‘that we might have it in common with him’, and Paul describes baptism as union with Christ (Romans 6:3–4; Galatians 3:26–27).

l.t: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.’
My Servant, in whom My soul delights; I will put My Spirit on Him.
If only You would rend the heavens and come down.
The Spirit of God hovering over the waters.
Matthew: John protests; ‘to fulfill all righteousness’.
Luke: Jesus was praying when heaven opened.
John the Baptist saw the Spirit come down and remain.
The curtain torn; the centurion: ‘Truly this man was the Son of God!’

qs: What three things happen as Jesus comes up out of the water?
Why do you think Jesus, who had no sin, chose to be baptized with sinners?
The Father says ‘You are My beloved Son’ before Jesus has done any public work. What does that say to you about God’s love?

1.h: The Temptation and Preaching of Jesus
1.ctx: Mark tells the testing in the wilderness in two verses, where Matthew and Luke describe three temptations (Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13). Then he jumps to Galilee after John’s arrest, a story he tells later (6:17–29), and gives a one-sentence summary of Jesus’ message.
1.mean: Straight after the Father’s words of love, the Spirit ‘drove’ Jesus into the wilderness. Mark’s word is forceful. It does not mean Jesus was unwilling; it shows the urgency of what must happen. Wesley observed that great moments of God’s favour are often followed by great testing. For forty days Jesus is ‘tempted by Satan’. Forty recalls Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, and the forty days of Moses and Elijah. Israel was tested in the wilderness and often failed; Jesus is tested and stands. Mark adds two details of his own. Jesus ‘was with the wild animals’, alone and far from human help, though they did him no harm. And ‘the angels ministered to Him’, as God cared for him. Mark does not describe a single dramatic victory. In his Gospel the battle with Satan goes on, as Jesus drives out demons again and again. Then Jesus comes into Galilee preaching ‘the gospel of God’. His message has two announcements and two commands. ‘The time is fulfilled’: the moment God promised has arrived. ‘The kingdom of God is near’: God is stepping in as King. The kingdom is not mainly a place on a map but God’s rule, his putting things right. It is ‘near’ because the King himself has come. So ‘Repent’: turn round, change direction. ‘And believe in the gospel’: trust the good news and commit yourself to it. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning, from sin and to God. Calvin noted that God both commands this turning and gives the power to do it. These two words sum up how anyone enters God’s kingdom.
1.big: Jesus is tested by Satan in the wilderness and stands firm, then announces that God’s promised time has come and his kingdom is near, calling everyone to repent and believe the good news.

vv.h: At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness
b: Matthew and Luke say Jesus was ‘led’; Mark says ‘drove’. Cooper connects it with Mark’s picture of Jesus as the Servant who goes where he is sent. Wesley drew a lesson: ‘extraordinary manifestations of his favour are wont to be followed by extraordinary temptations’. Calvin compared Jesus’ time apart to Moses being taken up Mount Sinai before he gave the Law: a withdrawal before a great public task.

vv.h: He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him
b: Only Mark mentions the animals. Calvin took the point to be loneliness: Jesus was ‘deprived of the kind offices of men, and was with the wild beasts’. Wesley adds, ‘Though they had no power to hurt him.’ Some see a hint of the peace of God’s coming kingdom, when ‘the wolf will live with the lamb’ (Isaiah 11:6); English thinks Mark may hint at this without claiming it is fulfilled. Both readings can be held together: the wilderness is a place of danger, and Jesus is safe in his Father’s care.

vv.h: After the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee
b: John’s work is done, and Mark will tell how it ended (6:17–29). John’s Gospel shows the two ministries overlapping for a while before this (John 3:22–24); Mark simply moves the spotlight to Jesus. Galilee was not a quiet backwater: it was busy, mixed and full of trade routes (English).

vv.h: The time is fulfilled … and the kingdom of God is near
b: ‘Fulfilled’ means the waiting is over. Wesley: ‘The time of my kingdom, foretold by Daniel, expected by you, is fully come.’ The Old Testament says both that God is King now (Isaiah 43:15) and that one day his rule will be seen by all (Zechariah 14:9). In Jesus the future reign begins to arrive in the present (English). It is ‘near’ because it is breaking in through Jesus himself, though it is not yet complete.

vv.h: Repent and believe in the gospel!
b: Repent means to change direction, not only to feel guilty (English). Believe means to trust and commit yourself, not just to agree. Calvin asked why Mark puts repentance and faith side by side, and answered that God commands us to turn and also gives the grace to do it: ‘not only is our duty enjoined on us, but the grace and power of obedience are, at the same time, offered.’ How God’s grace and our response fit together is a question Christians answer differently (see the notes on election in Romans 9 and Ephesians 1); the call itself to repent and believe is plain and urgent.

Israel was ‘tested’ forty years in the wilderness to see whether they would keep God’s commands (Deuteronomy 8:2), and they often failed. Jesus, God’s true Son, is tested and remains faithful. Hebrews says that because he was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15).

The kingdom of God is the heart of Jesus’ preaching in Mark (4:11, 26, 30; 9:1; 10:14–15; 14:25). Daniel saw a kingdom given by God that ‘will never be destroyed’ (Daniel 2:44; 7:14). Jesus announces that it has come near in him.

l.t: Israel tested forty years in the wilderness.
The wolf with the lamb: peace in the coming kingdom.
An everlasting kingdom given to one like a Son of Man.
Matthew: the three temptations and Jesus’ move to Capernaum.
Luke: the temptations, and Jesus returns in the power of the Spirit.
Tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.
Paul’s summary: repentance toward God and faith in Jesus.

qs: What details does Mark give about Jesus’ time in the wilderness that Matthew and Luke do not?
What do ‘repent’ and ‘believe’ each mean, and why does Jesus put them together?
Where do you sense God’s rule ‘coming near’ in your own life, and what turning might it ask of you?

1.ctx: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about fourteen miles long (Cooper), and Capernaum on its shore was a busy fishing town. Mark does not say whether these men had met Jesus before; John’s Gospel says Andrew and Simon first met him through John the Baptist (John 1:35–42).
1.mean: Jesus does not work alone. Almost the first thing he does is call people to be with him. Walking by the lake, he sees two brothers, Simon and Andrew, throwing a circular net into the water. ‘Come, follow Me,’ he says, ‘and I will make you fishers of men.’ And ‘at once’ they leave their nets and follow him. A little farther on he sees two more brothers, James and John, mending nets in their father Zebedee’s boat. He calls them too, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men and go after Jesus. Notice how the call works. Jesus takes the initiative: he sees them and calls them. They do not volunteer; he chooses them. His words are short and personal: ‘follow Me’. He calls them to himself, not just to a set of teachings. And he speaks their language. They catch fish, so he promises to make them catch people. Fishing for people is about gathering them for God. Notice, too, what it costs. Simon and Andrew leave their livelihood. James and John leave their business and their father. The hired men may suggest a working business, so the loss is real. Mark tells it simply, without explaining what was going on in their minds. He wants you to see the authority of Jesus’ call and the rightness of their response. This scene sets the pattern for discipleship throughout Mark. Being a disciple means being with Jesus, learning from him and going where he sends you (3:14). The first disciples will often fail to understand him, but they have taken the first step. Following Jesus starts here, with a word from him and a step after him.
1.big: Jesus calls four fishermen with the words ‘follow Me’, and they leave their work and family at once to be with him and learn to gather people for God.

vv.h: casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen
b: The detail of the net, and the view from the boat in the next scene, read like an eyewitness memory. English suggests the story is told from the fishermen’s side, perhaps as Peter remembered it. Early tradition links Mark’s Gospel with Peter’s preaching (see the introduction to Mark).

vv.h: Come, follow Me … and I will make you fishers of men
b: In the Old Testament, fishing for people is a picture of judgment: ‘I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them’ (Jeremiah 16:16; compare Amos 4:2; Habakkuk 1:14–17). Cooper sees an urgent rescue in Jesus’ words: people must be gathered before judgment comes. English, following Cranfield, thinks Jesus uses the image mainly because these men were fishermen, giving an old picture a new and hopeful meaning. Either way, Jesus promises to ‘make’ them: he will form them for the task.

vv.h: And at once they left their nets and followed Him
b: ‘At once’ (or ‘immediately’) is one of Mark’s favourite words, and it gives the whole Gospel its urgent pace. Wesley: ‘Happy they who follow Christ at the first call!’ Calvin noted that the Gospel writers did not always keep events in strict order of time, so Luke can place the miraculous catch of fish (Luke 5:1–11) alongside this call.

vv.h: they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men
b: Cooper notes that they broke family ties and tradition by leaving their father. Mark does not suggest they abandoned him; there are hired men to help. But Jesus’ call comes first. Later Jesus promises that whoever leaves home or family for his sake will receive far more (10:29–30). The ESV Study Bible points out that several of Jesus’ first disciples were not poor: James and John were part of a family business that employed others.

When God called Elisha through Elijah, Elisha asked first to kiss his parents goodbye (1 Kings 19:19–21). Jesus’ call is even more urgent (Luke 9:59–62). The pattern of call and response runs through the Bible: Abraham, Moses, the prophets, and now these fishermen.

In Mark the Twelve are appointed ‘to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach’ (3:14). Their story is not one of instant success; they misunderstand and fail. But it begins with Jesus’ call, and it ends with a promise that he will go ahead of them (16:7).

l.t: I will send for many fishermen, and they will catch them.
Elijah calls Elisha from his ploughing.
Matthew’s account of the same call.
Luke: the great catch of fish and Peter’s ‘Go away from me, Lord.’
Andrew brings his brother Simon to Jesus.
Called to be with him and to be sent out.
‘We have left everything to follow You.’

qs: What did each pair of brothers leave behind to follow Jesus?
Jesus calls them to follow him personally, not just to learn his teaching. What is the difference?
What ‘nets’ might Jesus be asking you to put down to follow him more closely?

1.ctx: Capernaum, a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, becomes Jesus’ base in Galilee. In the synagogue on the Sabbath, a visiting teacher could be invited to speak (Cooper; compare Acts 13:15). This is the first miracle Mark records.
1.mean: Mark’s first scene of Jesus at work shows his authority in two ways: in what he says and in what he does. On the Sabbath Jesus teaches in the synagogue at Capernaum, and the people are ‘astonished’. Mark tells you why: he taught ‘as one who had authority, and not as the scribes’. The scribes were the trained experts in the Law, and their teaching leaned on what earlier teachers had said. Jesus speaks with his own authority, as if God’s word were coming directly from him. Then a man with an ‘unclean spirit’, a demon, cries out. The spirit knows exactly who Jesus is: ‘Jesus of Nazareth’, an ordinary man from an ordinary town, and ‘the Holy One of God’. It knows why he has come, too: ‘Have You come to destroy us?’ Jesus does not argue or use a formula. Cooper notes that exorcists of the time often called on some higher power by name. Jesus simply commands: ‘Be silent!’ … ‘Come out of him!’ The spirit throws the man into convulsions, shrieks and leaves. Now the crowd are amazed again: ‘A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!’ His word and his deed go together. The same authority that teaches also sets people free. Why does Jesus silence the spirit when it has said something true? Calvin and Wesley answer that he would not accept testimony from evil powers or let people think he was in league with them (see 1:34). Mark wants you to notice something uncomfortable: the demon recognises Jesus before the people do. Knowing who Jesus is matters, but on its own it is not enough; even demons know. What Jesus looks for is faith and following. Here the kingdom Jesus just announced (1:15) begins to push back the powers that spoil human lives.
1.big: In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus teaches with his own authority and, with a word, drives out an evil spirit, showing that God’s kingdom has come to set people free.

vv.h: He taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes
b: Cooper explains that the scribes usually supported their views by quoting earlier authorities, while Jesus did not. Calvin saw the difference as spiritual power: Christ’s preaching shone with the power of the Spirit. Mark is contrasting Jesus’ manner of teaching with that of the scribes, not condemning Judaism. Mark does not say what Jesus taught here; the summary in 1:15 gives the heart of it. The ESV Study Bible suggests these may have been local scribes, learned men who taught in the synagogues, rather than the higher-ranking scribes ‘who had come down from Jerusalem’ to challenge Jesus (3:22).

vv.h: a man with an unclean spirit
b: ‘Unclean’ is Mark’s usual description of demons: they are opposed to God’s holiness and they defile and harm people. The Gospel writers distinguish between illness and possession (for example 1:34), though the two sometimes overlap. English urges restraint both ways: not every problem should be blamed on demons, but the Gospels’ account of real evil powers should not be dismissed either.

vv.h: I know who You are—the Holy One of God!
b: The spirit uses Jesus’ full identity, perhaps trying to gain power over him, since names were thought to give control (Cooper). Calvin thought it was a trick: the devil names Christ ‘to insinuate into the minds of men a suspicion, that there was some secret understanding between him and Christ’. ‘Us’ shows the spirit speaks for the whole evil realm: Jesus’ coming means their defeat.

vv.h: Be silent!
b: Wesley explained that Jesus ‘needed not their testimony, nor would encourage it, lest any should infer that he acted in concert with them.’ This is the first of several commands to silence in Mark (see the history note at 1:40).

vv.h: A new teaching with authority!
b: The crowd connect the teaching and the exorcism: both show the same authority. Mark uses several different words for people’s amazement at Jesus (English counts six). Amazement is not yet faith, but it is a beginning.

1.diff: Possession or illness? Some readers, such as the physician Dr Mead in Wesley’s day, have held that the ‘demoniacs’ of the Gospels were simply people with illnesses. Wesley rejected that view, noting that it makes Jesus forbid diseases to speak (note on 1:34). Calvin, Wesley and Cooper take the Gospels to describe real evil spirits. Donald English takes a middle path: the phrase may describe possession or ‘the source of a particular form of illness’, and the way people describe their experiences is not always correct, so not every problem should be blamed on demons; yet dismissing demonic activity is ‘too easy’, since the Gospel writers clearly distinguished illness from possession.

b: Jesus’ authority over evil spirits shows that ‘the strong man’ is being tied up (3:27). Later Jesus gives the Twelve authority to drive out demons (3:15; 6:7). The New Testament says the Son of God appeared ‘to destroy the works of the devil’ (1 John 3:8).

‘The Holy One of God’ is a title used of a person set apart for God (compare Aaron in Psalm 106:16). In John 6:69 Peter uses the same words of Jesus: the demon’s confession becomes a disciple’s confession.

l.t: Luke’s account of the same exorcism.
The crowds astonished at his authority after the Sermon on the Mount.
Binding the strong man.
Peter: ‘You are the Holy One of God.’
Even the demons believe, and shudder.
The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
Christ disarmed the powers and authorities.

qs: What two things amaze the people in the synagogue?
The demon knows who Jesus is. Why is that not the same as faith?
Where do you need to trust Jesus’ authority over what spoils your life or the lives of others?

b: Capernaum, on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, was very small compared with nearby Magdala, but it stood on the road to Damascus and was a centre of fishing and trade with a Roman tax station. A Roman milestone was found about 100 metres from the synagogue. The synagogue whose ruins stand today dates from the 4th or 5th century AD (about 10,000 coins were found beneath its floor), but below it lie the foundations of an older building, likely the synagogue mentioned in Luke 7:4–5, standing in Jesus’ day.

b: Just south of the synagogue is an octagonal building used in earlier centuries as a church. Within its walls are the stones of an earlier house, which the excavators think was Peter’s (Mark 1:29), and Italian archaeologists report deciphering Peter’s name among letters inscribed on the walls. This is the excavators’ identification; the source read for these notes reports it without saying how widely other scholars accept it.

1.ctx: This is still the same Sabbath. Jesus goes from the synagogue to the house Simon (Peter) shared with Andrew. Jewish days ran from sunset to sunset, and carrying burdens was forbidden on the Sabbath, so the townspeople wait until the Sabbath ends at sunset before bringing their sick.
1.mean: From the public synagogue Mark takes you into a private home. Simon’s mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. (So Peter was married; Paul later mentions that Peter took his wife on his travels, 1 Corinthians 9:5.) The disciples tell Jesus about her straight away. Mark describes what Jesus did with gentle detail: ‘He went to her, took her by the hand, and helped her up.’ He does not just speak a word from a distance; he comes close and touches her. The fever leaves her, and the healing is so complete that she immediately ‘began to serve them’. That is more than a sign that she felt better. In Mark, serving is the mark of a true disciple; Jesus himself ‘did not come to be served, but to serve’ (10:45). Then the sun goes down, the Sabbath is over, and the whole town comes to the door. People bring all who are sick and those troubled by demons. Jesus heals many and drives out many demons. But again he will not let the demons speak, ‘because they knew who He was’. Why the silence? Calvin and Wesley answer that Jesus would not have his identity announced by evil powers. And as the next scene shows, he does not want people flocking to him only as a miracle worker. Cooper suggests he wanted to show by word and deed what kind of Messiah he was before declaring it openly. Wesley imagined the hopeful scene at the door: ‘Who could then have imagined that all these blossoms would die away without fruit?’ The crowds will not last. But on this evening, God’s kingdom is visible in a small town, through healing hands and a Saviour who comes close.
1.big: Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law with a touch, and she rises to serve; that evening he heals many and silences the demons who know who he is.

vv.h: the home of Simon and Andrew
b: Wesley takes the house of 2:1 to be Peter’s, and Cooper calls Capernaum Jesus’ base of operations in Galilee. A house under a later church at Capernaum has been identified by its excavators as Peter’s; see the history note at 1:21.

vv.h: He went to her, took her by the hand, and helped her up
b: Cooper notes that Jesus could simply have spoken, but chose to touch: he enters into people’s pain. Cooper notes that fever could be read as a punishment from God for breaking the covenant (Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:22).

vv.h: she began to serve them
b: English sees obedient service as the mark of discipleship in Mark’s Gospel. Healing is not for comfort alone; it frees people to live for God and others. Mark later names women who followed Jesus and ‘ministered to Him’ in Galilee (15:41).

vv.h: That evening, after sunset
b: The Sabbath was over. Wesley: the Sabbath ‘which they reckoned from sunset to sunset.’ The people had respected the Sabbath rules by waiting; now they come in crowds.

vv.h: He would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was
b: Calvin offered two reasons: a general one, ‘because the time of the full revelation was not yet come’, and a special one, that Jesus refused such witnesses, whose praise could only harm his reputation. Cooper adds that Jesus wanted to show by word and deed what kind of Messiah he was before declaring himself openly. Mark repeats the theme (3:11–12).

Matthew, telling this same evening, quotes Isaiah: ‘He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases’ (Matthew 8:17, quoting Isaiah 53:4). How far Christ’s death secures physical healing now is discussed in the note on Matthew 8:14–17.
Jesus’ healings anticipate the day when God will wipe away every tear and there will be no more death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Each healing in Mark is a small sign of that coming world.

l.t: Matthew: ‘He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.’
Luke: Jesus rebuked the fever.
He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows.
The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve.
Peter (Cephas) takes along a believing wife.
Unclean spirits cry ‘You are the Son of God!’ and are silenced.
No more death, mourning or pain.

qs: What does Simon’s mother-in-law do as soon as she is healed?
Why do you think Jesus would not let the demons say who he was?
How might Jesus’ care for you set you free to serve someone else this week?

1.ctx: This is the morning after the busy Sabbath in Capernaum. Mark mentions Jesus praying alone three times, each at a turning point: here, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32–42).
1.mean: After a day and evening of teaching, healing and driving out demons, Jesus gets up while it is still dark and goes out to a solitary place to pray. This tells you something important about him. He is the Son of God, yet he needs time alone with his Father. His full humanity is real: he grows tired and he prays. And it tells you where his strength and direction come from. Before the crowds can shape his plans, he seeks his Father’s will. Meanwhile Simon and the others ‘went to look for Him’. Mark’s word suggests they hunted him down, perhaps anxiously or impatiently. When they find him, they say, ‘Everyone is looking for You!’ It sounds like good news. The whole town wants more. Surely this is the moment to stay and build on success? Jesus’ answer surprises them: ‘Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.’ He turns away from popularity. His main purpose is not to be the town’s healer but to announce the good news of God’s kingdom to as many as possible. The healings are real acts of love, and they show the kingdom’s power, but they serve the message rather than replacing it. Calvin noted that Jesus wanted people to be ‘more attentive to the word than to signs’ (his comment on 1:45). ‘That is why I have come’ may mean simply that this is why he came out from Capernaum. But Mark’s readers already know that Jesus has come from God, and the phrase may hint at that larger sending (compare 10:45). So Jesus sets off through Galilee, preaching in synagogues and driving out demons. Prayer gave him clarity, and clarity gave him the freedom to say no to the crowd and yes to his mission.
1.big: Jesus rises early to pray, then refuses to stay where he is popular, because his purpose is to preach the good news in town after town.

vv.h: Early in the morning, while it was still dark
b: Wesley: ‘So did he labour for us, both day and night.’ Cooper and English both see here Jesus’ real humanity and his dependence on his Father. English notes that Mark records Jesus praying at crucial moments, each before a new step in his mission.

vv.h: Everyone is looking for You!
b: Cooper suggests the disciples were caught up in Jesus’ rising popularity and wanted him to seize the moment. Calvin compared the Gospels: Mark mentions Peter’s words, Luke that the crowds came out to find him (Luke 4:42).

vv.h: Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come
b: Luke’s version reads, ‘that is why I was sent’ (Luke 4:43). Calvin saw here Jesus’ ‘earnest desire to fulfill his office’. English thinks ‘come’ means ‘come from God’, though he admits it is uncertain whether the disciples understood that. Preaching the good news is at the centre of Jesus’ mission (1:14–15).

vv.h: preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons
b: Mark’s summary joins word and deed again, as at Capernaum (1:21–28). The synagogue was where Scripture was read and explained each Sabbath, the natural place to announce that God’s promises were being fulfilled.
Jesus’ habit of withdrawing to pray is stronger still in Luke (Luke 5:16; 6:12; 9:18). Hebrews describes him praying ‘with loud cries and tears’ in the days of his earthly life (Hebrews 5:7).

The tension between meeting people’s needs and keeping to the central message appears again in Acts, when the apostles appoint others to serve tables so they can give themselves to prayer and the word (Acts 6:2–4).

l.t: Luke: ‘I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well.’
Matthew’s summary of Jesus’ ministry throughout Galilee.
After the feeding of the five thousand, he went up to pray.
Gethsemane: ‘Not what I will, but what You will.’
He often withdrew to lonely places to pray.
Prayers with loud cries and tears; he learned obedience.
Prayer and the ministry of the word.

qs: What does Jesus do before dawn, and what do the disciples want him to do when they find him?
Why do you think Jesus left a town where ‘everyone’ was looking for him?
How might time alone with God help you see what matters most when others are pulling you in different directions?

1.ctx: ‘Leprosy’ in the Bible covers a range of serious skin diseases, not only what is now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease). The Law required a person with such a disease to live apart, wear torn clothes and cry ‘Unclean, unclean!’ (Leviticus 13:45–46). A priest had to examine anyone healed and offer the sacrifices of Leviticus 14 before they could return to normal life.
1.mean: A man with leprosy does something he was not supposed to do: he comes right up to Jesus. The Law kept such people at a distance, cut off from family, worship and touch. He kneels and begs: ‘If You are willing, You can make me clean.’ He does not doubt that Jesus is able. What he does not know is whether Jesus wants to. Perhaps years of rejection had taught him to expect a no. Then Mark tells you what Jesus felt and did. ‘Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man.’ To touch a leper was unthinkable: by the Law’s rules it made you unclean. Yet instead of the uncleanness passing to Jesus, the man is made clean. ‘I am willing,’ he says. ‘Be clean!’ And immediately the leprosy is gone. Jesus’ willingness answers the man’s deepest fear. Some ancient manuscripts say Jesus was ‘moved with indignation’ rather than compassion (see Where readings differ). If so, his anger was not at the man but at the disease and the misery it caused. Then Jesus sends the man away firmly with two instructions. Tell no one. And go to the priest and make the offering Moses commanded, ‘as a testimony to them’. Jesus respects the Law: the priest’s official verdict would prove the healing and restore the man to his community. But the man cannot keep quiet. He spreads the news everywhere, so that Jesus can no longer enter towns openly and has to stay in lonely places. Even there people come to him. The man’s joy is understandable, but disobeying Jesus has a cost. Jesus wanted room to preach, not crowds who came only for miracles. Still, the heart of the story shines clearly: Jesus is willing, and his touch makes the unclean clean.
1.big: Jesus touches and heals a man with leprosy, showing that he is willing to make the unclean clean, then sends him to the priest; the man’s disobedience to Jesus’ call for silence makes the crowds harder to escape.

vv.h: If You are willing, You can make me clean
b: In the Old Testament curing leprosy was treated as something for God alone; the king of Israel cried, ‘Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?’ (2 Kings 5:7). Calvin saw the significance of the reply: ‘He who, by the mere expression of his will, restores health to men, must possess supreme authority.’

vv.h: Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man
b: Cooper suggests Jesus touched the man first because he had not felt a human touch for a long time. By the Law’s rules, touching him should have made Jesus unclean; instead the man is cleansed. Jesus does not set the Law aside; he does what the Law could only diagnose and confirm.

vv.h: Jesus promptly sent him away with a stern warning
b: Mark’s words are strong. ‘Stern warning’ translates a verb of deep, almost wordless emotion, and ‘sent away’ is the verb Mark uses for driving out demons (English; Cooper). Jesus is deeply moved by suffering and determined that his mission should not be swallowed up by demand for miracles.

vv.h: show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them
b: See Leviticus 14:1–32. Calvin took ‘to them’ to mean the priests: their own verdict would leave them without excuse if they later rejected Jesus. Wesley adds that the priests could not later deny the healing once they had declared him clean. Wesley also draws a lesson for believers: ‘If he has made us clean from our leprosy of sin, we are not commanded to conceal it.’

vv.h: Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view
b: Calvin explained why Jesus had asked for silence: the people were so eager for miracles that there was no room left for teaching. ‘He wished that they would all be more attentive to the word than to signs.’ The healed man now moves freely in the towns while Jesus must stay outside them.

1.diff: ‘Moved with compassion’ or ‘moved with indignation’ (verse 41)? The BSB prints ‘compassion’; its footnote records that the SBL edition reads ‘indignation’. English notes that some early and reliable manuscripts have the word for anger and argues it is more likely original, because a copyist would be more likely to soften ‘anger’ to ‘compassion’ than the reverse; he takes it as anger at evil, not at the man. Cooper also prefers ‘being angered’, as anger at the disease as Satan’s work. The case for ‘compassion’ is that it is the reading the BSB keeps, the reading Calvin and Wesley both expounded, and it fits the story’s point that Jesus is willing to heal. Both readings show Jesus deeply moved by suffering, and Jesus’ anger at evil appears elsewhere in Mark (3:5).

b: The Law could identify uncleanness and declare someone clean once healed, but it could not cure (Leviticus 13–14). Elisha’s healing of Naaman was a famous exception (2 Kings 5). Jesus heals by his own word and touch.
By the end of the story the outsider has come in and Jesus stays outside. Hebrews says ‘Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood’ (Hebrews 13:12).

l.t: The person with a skin disease must live alone outside the camp.
The law for the day of cleansing.
Naaman healed of leprosy through Elisha.
Matthew’s account after the Sermon on the Mount.
Luke: the news spread, and Jesus withdrew to pray.
Ten lepers cleansed; one returns to give thanks.
Jesus suffered outside the gate.

qs: What does the man with leprosy believe about Jesus, and what is he unsure of?
Why was it so striking that Jesus touched the man before healing him?
Is there anything you hesitate to bring to Jesus because you are unsure he is willing? What does this story say to that fear?

hist.t: Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet? (the ‘messianic secret’)
b: Mark records a series of commands to silence: to demons (1:25, 34; 3:11–12), to people healed (1:44; 5:43; 7:36; 8:26) and to the disciples after Peter’s confession and the transfiguration (8:29–30; 9:9). In 1901 the German scholar William Wrede called this the ‘messianic secret’. He argued that Jesus did not understand himself to be the Messiah, that his followers came to see him so only after the resurrection, and that Mark took the secrecy theme over from his sources.

Other scholars, such as Albert Schweitzer, David Aune and Robert Stein, find this hard to accept. Stein points out that belief in the resurrection alone would not have made someone the Messiah, since Jewish hopes did not connect the Messiah with rising from the dead. Others offer historical reasons for real secrecy: ‘Messiah’ and ‘Son of God’ carried political dangers under Roman rule; Jesus’ mission would not be complete until his return; and he wanted the cross, not miracles, at the centre of what people understood about him. Mark itself notes the practical cost of publicity (1:45). The sources read here do not show a single majority explanation. The commentators used for these notes (English, Cooper, Calvin, Wesley) all treat the secrecy as Jesus’ own choice.
