2.ctx: Jesus is back in Capernaum, probably at Peter’s house (1:29). This is the first of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6) in which religious leaders object to what Jesus says and does, ending with a plot to kill him (3:6). Houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair. The Old Testament teaches that forgiving sins belongs to God (Exodus 34:7; Isaiah 43:25).
2.mean: The house is so packed that nobody else can get near the door. Jesus is speaking God’s word to them, the good news of God’s kingdom. Four men arrive carrying a paralysed friend on a mat. They cannot get in, so they climb onto the roof, dig through it and lower him down right in front of Jesus. Jesus sees ‘their faith’, the faith that would not give up, and then says something nobody expects: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’ They came for healing; Jesus starts with forgiveness. He goes to the deepest need first. Some scribes sitting there are shocked. ‘He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?’ They are right about one thing: only God can forgive sins against him. If Jesus is only a man, he has claimed what belongs to God. Jesus knows what they are thinking and asks a sharp question: which is easier, to tell a paralysed man his sins are forgiven, or to tell him to get up and walk? Saying ‘your sins are forgiven’ is easy, because nobody can see whether it has happened. Saying ‘get up and walk’ is tested on the spot. So Jesus does the visible thing to prove the invisible: ‘so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…’ He tells the man to get up, pick up his mat and go home. The man stands, picks up his mat and walks out in front of everyone. The crowd are astounded and praise God; they have never seen anything like it. Mark wants you to face the scribes’ question. Either Jesus is a blasphemer, or he has the authority of God himself. The healing settles which it is. And the forgiveness the man received is offered to everyone who comes to Jesus, whether or not they are carried there by friends.
2.big: Jesus forgives a paralysed man’s sins and then heals him, proving that he, the Son of Man, has God’s authority on earth to forgive.

vv.h: they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat
b: Wesley explains that flat roofs had a covering or trap door, which the friends took up and then ‘broke the passage wider’ to let the mat through. Cooper pictures the falling debris and the shock to the house owner. Mark tells it simply; the effort itself shows how much they believed Jesus could help. The ESV Study Bible describes such a roof as branches or sticks combined with clay; Luke adds that this one had tiles (Luke 5:19).

vv.h: When Jesus saw their faith
b: Whose faith? The four friends’ certainly. Calvin thought ‘their’ also included the paralysed man, because ‘the paralytic could not have obtained the forgiveness of his sins, if he had had no faith of his own.’ English thinks it more likely that the sick man shared it too. Calvin added that faith was visible in their ‘laboriousness’: they would not have taken such trouble without confidence in Jesus. The faith of friends can bring someone to Jesus; each person must still receive his forgiveness for themselves.

vv.h: Son, your sins are forgiven
b: ‘Son’ is a word of affection. Was the man’s illness caused by sin? Jesus does not say so, and elsewhere he denies that suffering is always punishment for a person’s own sin (John 9:2–3). Calvin thought Jesus went to the root of all human trouble, our separation from God, before dealing with the symptom. Cooper notes that in Mark this is the only place where Jesus explicitly forgives someone’s sins.

vv.h: He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?
b: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him. Calvin thought the scribes were too quick to take the worst meaning, since prophets also announced God’s forgiveness. Wesley saw the first opposition coming from the learned, not from ordinary people: ‘See whence the first offense cometh!’ The same charge of blasphemy will be Jesus’ death sentence (14:64).

vv.h: Which is easier
b: English explains: it is easier to say ‘your sins are forgiven’, because no one can check it; to say ‘get up and walk’ is to face an immediate test. Cooper puts it the other way round: saying either is easy, but doing either is impossible without God’s power. Both readings reach the same point: the healing is visible proof of the forgiveness.

vv.h: the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
b: This is the first time Jesus calls himself ‘the Son of Man’ in Mark; he will use the title often. The phrase can mean simply a human being, as in Psalm 8:4, but English thinks it more likely draws on Daniel’s vision of ‘One like the Son of Man’ who is given ‘dominion, glory, and kingship’ (Daniel 7:13–14). The one who will judge at the end can forgive now, ‘on earth’.

vv.h: We have never seen anything like this!
b: Isaiah had promised that in the age of salvation ‘the lame will leap like a deer’ (Isaiah 35:6). The people glorify God, as they should, though they do not yet grasp who Jesus is. English notes that even here there is no compelling proof: people still had to take Jesus’ word for the forgiveness. Faith is invited, not forced.

The Psalms join forgiveness and healing: God is the one ‘who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases’ (Psalm 103:3). Jesus does both, and in that order. God says, ‘I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions’ (Isaiah 43:25); Jesus does what God does.
After his resurrection Jesus gives his followers a share in declaring forgiveness in his name (John 20:23); the authority behind it remains his (1 John 1:9).

l.t: He forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.
God blots out transgressions for his own sake.
One like the Son of Man given dominion.
The lame will leap like a deer.
Matthew: the crowd praised God for giving such authority to men.
Luke: Pharisees and teachers had come from every village.
Suffering is not always punishment for one’s own sin.
The charge of blasphemy at Jesus’ trial.

qs: What did the four friends do to get the paralysed man to Jesus, and what did Jesus say first?
Why were the scribes right that only God can forgive sins, and what does that mean for who Jesus is?
Who might you ‘carry’ to Jesus through prayer, friendship or practical help?

2.ctx: Mark places the booth ‘beside the sea’, probably at or near Capernaum, which lay on the road to Damascus and had a tax post. Tax collectors in Galilee worked under Herod Antipas’s system and were often seen as extortioners (English). Matthew’s Gospel tells the same story about ‘Matthew’ (Matthew 9:9), and lists Matthew the tax collector among the Twelve (Matthew 10:3).
2.mean: Jesus is teaching by the lake again, and as he walks along he sees Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at his tax booth. ‘Follow Me,’ Jesus says, and Levi gets up and follows him. Mark tells it in one breath, just as he told the call of the fishermen. But this call is more shocking. Fishermen were respectable working men. Tax collectors were seen as traitors who grew rich at their neighbours’ expense. Calvin saw Levi’s call as an example of ‘Christ’s undeserved goodness’: Jesus calls people not because they are good, but because he is gracious. Then comes a dinner at Levi’s house. ‘Many tax collectors and sinners’ are there, eating with Jesus and his disciples. ‘Sinners’ here means people known for not keeping God’s law, or for not keeping the Pharisees’ strict rules about it. Eating together meant friendship and acceptance, so the scribes who were Pharisees are offended. They ask the disciples, ‘Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?’ Jesus answers with a proverb and a statement of his mission. ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.’ A doctor who avoided sick people would be useless. ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.’ Jesus is not saying the Pharisees had no need of him. He is saying that only those who know they are sick will come to the doctor. The people who thought they were fine kept their distance; the people who knew they were not came to the table. Jesus’ welcome does not mean he approves of everything they did; Levi left his booth behind. But the welcome comes first. Mark wants you to see that no one is too far gone for Jesus to call, and that the only thing that keeps anyone from his table is thinking they do not need it.
2.big: Jesus calls a despised tax collector to follow him and eats with sinners, because he came, like a doctor, for those who know they are sick.

vv.h: Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth
b: Levi is identified with the Matthew of Matthew 9:9, the traditional identification, which English accepts. English notes a small puzzle: Mark also calls James ‘son of Alphaeus’ (3:18), and he does not explain whether Levi and James were brothers. English explains that tax collectors in Galilee worked for Herod Antipas’s system and mostly extorted more than was required. The ESV Study Bible suggests that a tax booth ‘beside the sea’ (2:13) was used for taxing fishermen.

vv.h: Follow Me
b: The same call as to the fishermen (1:17), and the same immediate response. Cooper notes that Levi left behind a very profitable business. English sees in Levi someone used to making hard decisions and living with them.

vv.h: many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him and His disciples
b: Wesley thought some were ‘doubtless invited by Matthew’ out of concern for his old friends, while many simply pressed in uninvited because they wanted to hear Jesus. The BSB reads ‘Levi’s house’; English notes that the original says only ‘his house’, which could also mean the house where Jesus was staying. At a formal meal guests reclined on couches around the table, and the ESV Study Bible notes that reclining together showed personal acceptance and friendship.

vv.h: the scribes who were Pharisees
b: The Pharisees were a movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law, including rules about food and purity. Cooper notes that to them ‘sinners’ included anyone who did not follow their interpretation of Scripture. Eating with such people risked uncleanness.

vv.h: It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick
b: Wesley read it as gentle irony: ‘if these were righteous I should not call them. But now, they are the very persons I came to save.’ Calvin said the scribes erred in two ways: they forgot what Christ had come to do, and they excused their own faults while despising others. Matthew adds Jesus’ words from Hosea, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’ (Matthew 9:13; Hosea 6:6).

Jesus’ meals with outsiders run through the Gospels: he is called ‘a friend of tax collectors and sinners’ (Luke 7:34). Luke tells of another tax collector, Zacchaeus, and Jesus’ words: ‘the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost’ (Luke 19:10).

Paul calls himself the worst of sinners and says Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The doctor image runs back to God’s words to Israel: ‘I am the LORD who heals you’ (Exodus 15:26).

l.t: Matthew: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’
Luke: Levi held a great banquet; ‘sinners to repentance’.
I desire mercy, not sacrifice.
Tax collectors and sinners draw near; the lost sheep.
Zacchaeus: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.
Levi’s fellow disciples: the Twelve.

qs: Who comes to Levi’s dinner, and who objects?
What does Jesus mean by comparing himself to a doctor? Who are ‘the healthy’?
Are there people you find it hard to imagine Jesus calling? What does Levi’s story say to you about them, and about yourself?

b: Capernaum stood on the road linking the region with Damascus, and the Lexham Bible Dictionary describes it as a centre of commerce and a Roman tax station; a Roman milestone has been found near its synagogue. If Levi’s booth was in Capernaum (Mark does not name the town), it fits what is known of it. See the history note on Capernaum at Mark 1:21.

2.ctx: The Law commanded a fast only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Pious Pharisees fasted much more often, twice a week (Luke 18:12), which English and Cooper say was Mondays and Thursdays. John the Baptist’s disciples also fasted; English suggests their teacher’s imprisonment (1:14) may have given them a particular reason.
2.mean: Fasting means going without food for a time, usually to pray, to mourn or to show sorrow for sin. John’s disciples and the Pharisees fasted often. Jesus’ disciples did not, and people noticed: ‘Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?’ Jesus answers with a picture everyone knew: a wedding. Cooper notes that a wedding was a time of feasting and great joy. Nobody fasts at a wedding while the bridegroom is there. ‘How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?’ Jesus speaks of himself as the bridegroom (Calvin: he ‘compares himself to the bridegroom’), and his coming is a time of joy, not mourning. In the Old Testament, God himself is pictured as the bridegroom or husband of his people: ‘as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you’ (Isaiah 62:5). English suggests Jesus may be hinting at that role, though only the eye of faith would see it then. Then the mood changes: ‘But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.’ Cooper calls this the first indication in Mark that Jesus was fully aware of his mission, and English sees a hint of Jesus’ death. The joy of his presence will be followed by sorrow, and the disciples will fast then. So Jesus is not against fasting. He is against fasting as a fixed rule that ignores what God is doing. Fasting fits times of waiting, longing and sorrow; it does not fit the moment when the long-awaited bridegroom has arrived. Calvin drew out a lesson for Christians: do not make outward practices a test of holiness, and do not try to make everyone follow your own pattern of devotion. The early church did fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23), in the time between Jesus’ going away and his coming again. Christians still live in that time: the bridegroom has been ‘taken’, and they long for his return, yet he is with them by his Spirit.
2.big: Jesus’ disciples do not fast because the bridegroom has come, a time for joy, but he warns that he will be taken away and then they will fast.

vv.h: Why don’t Your disciples fast
b: Calvin thought the Pharisees were trying to stir up rivalry between John’s disciples and Jesus’ disciples, and warned against breaking the unity of faith over outward ceremonies. Cooper notes that some Pharisees made sure others saw them fasting (compare Matthew 6:16–18).

vv.h: How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?
b: The BSB’s ‘guests’ translates a Hebrew-style phrase, which Calvin explains as a Hebrew phrase, ‘the children of the bridegroom, or of the nuptial bed’, meaning the wedding guests. Calvin says Christ ‘compares himself to the bridegroom’. John the Baptist had called Jesus the bridegroom and himself the bridegroom’s friend (John 3:29). The Old Testament pictures God as Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19).

vv.h: the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them
b: Cooper calls this the first indication in Mark that Jesus knew where his mission would lead; English agrees that it hints at Jesus’ death. Calvin noted that Jesus was easing his disciples into hardship gradually, sparing them while he was with them. The ESV Study Bible hears an echo of the Servant who ‘was taken away’ (Isaiah 53:8).
The prophets looked forward to the day when fasts would become feasts (Zechariah 8:19). Jesus’ coming begins that joy, though the full wedding feast lies ahead (Revelation 19:7–9).

Jesus assumes his followers will fast (Matthew 6:16–18), and the early church fasted when seeking God’s guidance (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Christians differ in how they practise it, for example in set seasons such as Lent or in personal times of prayer, but in Scripture fasting goes with prayer and seeking God (Acts 13:2–3).

l.t: As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
I will betroth you to Me forever.
The fasts will become joyful feasts.
Matthew: ‘Can the guests of the bridegroom mourn?’
Luke’s account of the same question.
John the Baptist: the friend of the bridegroom.
The wedding supper of the Lamb.
The church at Antioch fasts and prays.

qs: Why, according to Jesus, do his disciples not fast while he is with them?
What does Jesus mean by calling himself the bridegroom, and what does ‘taken from them’ point to?
Is there a spiritual practice you treat as a rule for its own sake? How might it help you seek God instead?

2.ctx: Jesus continues his answer about fasting with two everyday pictures. Wine was stored in skins, and new wine, still fermenting, needed flexible skins that could expand (Cooper). Luke adds a third saying about old wine (Luke 5:39).
2.mean: Jesus finishes his answer with two pictures from ordinary life. First, the patch. If you sew a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat, the first time it gets wet the new patch shrinks, pulls away and makes the tear worse. Second, the wineskins. New wine is still fermenting. Pour it into old, dried-out, brittle skins and the gas will burst them, and you lose both the wine and the skins. ‘Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.’ What is Jesus saying? Something new has arrived with him, and it cannot simply be added onto old ways of doing things. On the most common reading among the commentators used here (English, Cooper), the joy of the bridegroom’s presence does not fit the old pattern of regular fasting, just as new wine does not fit old skins, and more broadly the life of God’s kingdom needs a new shape. The forgiveness he offers (2:5), his welcome to sinners (2:17) and his authority over the Sabbath (2:28) all burst the old expectations. Notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say the old was bad. Old coats and old skins were good things. Jesus came to fulfil the Law and the Prophets, not to abolish them (Matthew 5:17), and English stresses that he is not saying the old should be discarded. But the new life he brings must be allowed to take its own shape. Christians have applied these pictures in different ways, and there is a real question about what exactly the old and new stand for (see Where readings differ). Calvin, for example, thought Jesus was talking about not loading new disciples with burdens they were not ready to bear. Either way, the sayings warn against forcing the life of God’s kingdom into old moulds, whether the strict rules of the Pharisees or our own habits and traditions.
2.big: With pictures of a patch and wineskins, Jesus teaches that the new life of God’s kingdom cannot be squeezed into old patterns; it needs new forms.

vv.h: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment
b: Cooper explains the picture: the unshrunk patch shrinks when washed and tears the old cloth. English: the old cannot simply absorb the new as an add-on; the new surpasses what went before, and the old should not force it into its own shape.

vv.h: new wine is poured into new wineskins
b: New wine needs flexible skins that can stretch as it ferments (Cooper). Wesley’s version notes that ‘bottles’ means ‘sacks of skin’. Luke adds that people who have drunk old wine prefer it (Luke 5:39); Calvin took this as a warning to the Pharisees not to give a received custom undue weight.

2.diff: What are the old and the new? English and Cooper take the old garment and old wineskins to be the existing pattern of religious practice (English: the structure of Jewish ceremonial), and the new cloth and new wine to be the life of the kingdom Jesus brings, which needs new forms. Cooper goes further, saying Jesus came not to reform Judaism but to bring something new, the church; English, by contrast, stresses that Jesus is not saying the old should be discarded, and Jesus himself said he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 5:17). Calvin rejected the view that the old garments stand for the Pharisees, saying it has ‘no probability on their side’. He read the sayings as being about Jesus’ disciples: they were new and weak, and must not be crushed by a stricter discipline than they could bear, so ‘we ought to spare the weak’. Both readings fit the setting of the fasting question.

b: The prophets promised something new from God: ‘Behold, I am about to do something new’ (Isaiah 43:19), and a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus later speaks of ‘the new covenant in My blood’ at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).

Paul wrestles with the same question in Galatians: whether the new life in Christ must be lived within the old forms of the Law. His answer is that ‘neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation’ (Galatians 6:15).

l.t: Matthew: both the new wine and the new wineskins are preserved.
Luke adds: ‘The old is better.’
Behold, I am about to do something new.
A new covenant written on the heart.
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.
What counts is a new creation.

qs: What happens when new cloth is sewn on an old garment, or new wine is put in old skins?
What ‘new thing’ in 2:1–20 does not fit the old patterns?
Are there habits or traditions in your life that make it hard for God to do something new?

2.ctx: God commanded Israel to rest on the seventh day, even at harvest time (Exodus 20:8–11; 34:21). The Law allowed a hungry traveller to pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25); the issue here is doing it on the Sabbath. Later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah (Shabbat 7:2), lists thirty-nine main kinds of forbidden work, with reaping among the first.
2.mean: On a Sabbath, Jesus and his disciples walk through a field, and the disciples pick heads of grain as they go. The Pharisees object that they are breaking the Sabbath. Picking grain was allowed on other days (Deuteronomy 23:25), but in the Pharisees’ view it counted as reaping, which was work, and work was forbidden on the Sabbath. Jesus answers from Scripture, reminding them what David did when he and his men were hungry. When David was fleeing from King Saul, the priest gave him the holy bread from the tabernacle, which by law only the priests could eat (1 Samuel 21:1–6; Leviticus 24:5–9). Human need came before the ritual rule, and Scripture does not condemn David. If David could do that, Jesus’ disciples are not guilty for picking grain when hungry. Then Jesus states a principle that only Mark records: ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.’ God gave the Sabbath as a gift: a day of rest, freedom and worship. It was meant to serve people, not to burden them with rules that defeat its purpose. Calvin noted that Jesus is not abolishing the Sabbath here, but showing ‘what is the proper use of it’. Finally comes the boldest claim: ‘Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.’ The Sabbath was God’s own day (Exodus 20:10). To be its Lord is to stand where God stands. As Wesley put it, the supreme Lawgiver has power over his own laws. Mark’s story is building: Jesus forgives sins, welcomes sinners, replaces fasting with feasting, and now claims authority over the Sabbath itself. In the next scene the Pharisees begin plotting to kill him (3:6). For Christians today the passage raises the question of how the Sabbath command applies now, and Christian traditions answer it differently (see the note on Matthew 12:1–8).
2.big: Defending his hungry disciples, Jesus teaches that the Sabbath was given for human good and claims that he, the Son of Man, is Lord even of the Sabbath.

vv.h: His disciples began to pick the heads of grain
b: The Mishnah, a later collection of Jewish legal rulings, lists sowing, ploughing, reaping, threshing, winnowing and grinding among the thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (Shabbat 7:2). Luke adds that the disciples rubbed the grain in their hands (Luke 6:1), which Cooper notes the Pharisees could count as threshing too.

vv.h: Have you never read what David did
b: Calvin: ‘If David’s necessity excused him, the same argument ought to be admitted in the case of others.’ He adds that Jesus takes for granted that David was blameless. English notes that Jesus does not defend breaking the Sabbath as such; he points to a principle that matters more, human need.

vv.h: During the high priesthood of Abiathar
b: In 1 Samuel 21 the priest who gave David the bread is Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar escaped Saul’s massacre of the priests soon after and became high priest under David (1 Samuel 22:20). How Mark’s wording fits 1 Samuel is discussed in Where readings differ.

vv.h: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath
b: Calvin notes that this saying is ‘related by Mark alone’, and that ‘they are mistaken, I think, who suppose that in this passage the Sabbath is entirely abolished; for Christ simply informs us what is the proper use of it.’ Wesley: the Sabbath was made for man ‘And therefore must give way to man’s necessity.’ English observes that the general point can also be found in rabbinic teaching; the new thing is who says it, and what he says next.

vv.h: Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath
b: Wesley: ‘Being the supreme Lawgiver, he hath power to dispense with his own laws’. English notes that ‘Son of Man’ can sometimes mean simply ‘a person’, but he and the other commentators read it here as Jesus speaking of himself, as in 2:10. Cooper sees here Jesus’ claim to lordship over the Law.

2.diff: Abiathar or Ahimelech (2:26)? In 1 Samuel 21 the priest is Ahimelech, but Mark’s Greek names Abiathar, his son. Readings: (1) ‘In the passage about Abiathar’. A. R. Millard (New Bible Dictionary) argues that the phrase is better rendered this way, as in Mark 12:26, where ‘about the burning bush’ refers to a section of Scripture. (2) ‘In the days of Abiathar’. Wesley read it as ‘In the time of Abiathar, who was afterward the high priest’: the events happened in Abiathar’s day, and he is named by the title he later held; the New Bible Dictionary notes that he was high priest during David’s reign. The ESV Study Bible accepts either of these first two readings. (3) A slip. English lists suggestions (a copyist’s addition, an early Jewish-style exposition of the story, or someone working from memory) and concludes, ‘It is a mistake’; he notes that some manuscripts leave out the phrase, as Matthew and Luke do. He argues that Mark faithfully kept what he received rather than smoothing it over.

b: The Sabbath was rooted in creation, when God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:11), and in rescue from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). It was a gift of rest. Isaiah calls it ‘a delight’ (Isaiah 58:13).

Hebrews says a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God, entered through faith in Christ (Hebrews 4:9–10). Christians gather on the first day of the week, the day of Jesus’ resurrection (Acts 20:7). How the fourth commandment applies to Christians is set out in the note on Matthew 12:1–8.

l.t: David receives the consecrated bread at Nob.
The Bread of the Presence, for Aaron and his sons.
Remember the Sabbath day: rooted in creation.
You may pluck heads of grain by hand.
Matthew adds the priests in the temple and ‘I desire mercy’.
Luke: the disciples rub the grain in their hands.
The next Sabbath conflict and the plot to kill Jesus.
A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.

qs: What did the disciples do, and why did the Pharisees object?
What does ‘the Sabbath was made for man’ tell you about why God gave the Sabbath?
How could a regular day of rest and worship become a gift to you rather than a burden?

3.ctx: Rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand was not urgent; it could wait a day.
3.mean: In the synagogue his opponents watch to see if he will heal on the Sabbath, ‘In order to accuse Jesus’. He calls the man to stand in front of everyone and asks: ‘Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?’ They are silent. ‘Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart.’ He heals the hand with a word, doing no ‘work’ at all. And the Pharisees go out to plot with the Herodians how to kill him: on the Sabbath, they plan to destroy life.
3.big: Refusing to do good is itself a choice for evil; and Jesus’ anger at hard hearts is mixed with grief.

b: The Herodians appear only in the Gospels (here, 12:13 and Matthew 22:16), and no ancient source describes them fully. They were apparently Jews who supported the rule of Herod’s family, and so, indirectly, Rome. Pharisees and Herodians normally had little in common; that they joined forces against Jesus shows how threatening both groups found him.

src.l: ‘Herodians’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

3.ctx: Idumea was far to the south, and Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast to the north-west. People were coming from every direction.
3.mean: Huge crowds come from all over the region. Jesus has a boat ready so they will not crush him, ‘For He had healed so many that all who had diseases were pressing forward to touch Him.’ Unclean spirits fall down and cry ‘You are the Son of God!’, but Jesus sternly orders them not to make him known.
3.big: Jesus did not accept testimony to himself from demons; he would make himself known in his own way and time.

3.ctx: Israel had twelve tribes. Choosing twelve signalled that Jesus was reconstituting God’s people around himself.
3.mean: On a mountain Jesus calls ‘those He wanted’ and appoints twelve: first ‘to accompany Him’, then ‘to be sent out to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons.’ Being with him comes before being sent. The list is a strange mixture: fishermen; a tax collector (Matthew); ‘Simon the Zealot’, whose name may mean he had been an anti-Roman nationalist; and ‘Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus’. Simon is renamed Peter (‘Rock’) and James and John ‘Sons of Thunder’.
3.big: Jesus chooses unlikely people, wants them first to be with him, and then sends them out.

3.ctx: ‘Beelzebul’ (‘lord of the house’) was a name for the prince of demons. The scribes ‘from Jerusalem’ were an official delegation.
3.mean: Jesus’ family come to ‘take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”’ The Jerusalem scribes have a worse explanation: ‘He is possessed by Beelzebul’. Jesus shows the absurdity: ‘How can Satan drive out Satan?’ A kingdom or house divided against itself cannot stand. Rather, ‘no one can enter a strong man’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man.’ Satan is the strong man; Jesus is the stronger one who has come to bind him and set his captives free.
3.big: Jesus’ exorcisms are not Satan’s tricks but Satan’s defeat.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 3:23–30 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: This saying follows directly on the scribes’ claim that Jesus’ work by the Spirit was the devil’s work.
3.mean: ‘Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter.’ The generosity is staggering. ‘But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.’ Mark explains why Jesus said it: ‘because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”’ The scribes saw God’s Spirit plainly at work and called it Satan.
3.big: Every sin can be forgiven, except the settled refusal that calls God’s saving work evil and so shuts the door on the only source of forgiveness.
3.diff: Christians broadly agree that this is not a careless word or a single sin a believer might commit by accident. Calvin says those who reject the Spirit’s work ‘after that the power of God has been revealed, cannot be excused on the plea of ignorance’. Wesley defined it as ‘ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil which Christ wrought by the power of the Holy Ghost’. Pastors in every tradition add that a person anxious about having committed it shows by that very anxiety that they have not.

3.ctx: This picks up the story from 3:21, where Jesus’ family set out to take him home.
3.mean: Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive and send for him. Looking at the people sitting around him, he says, ‘Here are My mother and My brothers! For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.’ He is not disowning his family (compare John 19:26–27), but he is defining a new family, bound together by doing God’s will.
3.big: Jesus’ followers become his family, closer even than blood.
3.diff: Who Jesus’ ‘brothers’ were is discussed at 6:1. Wesley noted that ‘neither did these of his brethren believe on him’ at this time (John 7:5), though James later became a leader in the church.

4.ctx: A parable is a short story from everyday life that carries a spiritual meaning. In Palestine seed was often scattered by hand and then ploughed in, so some inevitably fell on paths and stony patches.
4.mean: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells of a farmer whose seed falls in four places: on the path, where birds eat it; on rocky ground, where it springs up and withers; among thorns, which choke it; and on good soil, where it yields ‘thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold’. A good harvest was perhaps sevenfold to tenfold; these are extraordinary yields. ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’
4.big: Much of the sowing seems wasted, but the harvest will be astonishing.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 4:1–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: Verse 12 quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, where Isaiah is warned that his preaching will harden a stubborn people.
4.mean: Alone with the Twelve and others, Jesus says: ‘The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables, so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’’ Parables reveal and conceal at the same time. To those who come close and ask, they open up; to those who stay outside, they remain riddles.
4.big: The same word that opens the eyes of seekers leaves the indifferent more blind.
4.diff: Does God harden people? Reformed theology takes this as God’s judicial hardening: Calvin says the word ‘blinds and hardens the reprobate’, yet ‘through their own depravity’, as weak eyes are dazzled by the sun. Arminian (Wesleyan) theology stresses that the hardening follows human choice: Wesley wrote, ‘They would not see before now they could not, God having given them up to the blindness which they had chosen.’ Both agree that the hardened are responsible, and that the purpose of preaching is that people ‘might turn and be forgiven’.

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Mark 4

4.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained
4.ctx: This is one of the few parables Jesus explains point by point, giving a key for reading the others.
4.mean: ‘The farmer sows the word.’ The path is those from whom ‘Satan comes and takes away the word’. The rocky ground is those who receive it ‘with joy’ but have no root, and when trouble or persecution comes ‘they quickly fall away’. The thorns are those in whom ‘the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things’ choke the word. The good soil is those who ‘hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop’.
4.big: What matters is not a quick, joyful start but lasting fruit; and the threats are Satan, suffering and the cares and riches of life.
4.diff: Rocky ground and falling away. Reformed readers take the rocky and thorny soils as people who never truly had saving faith, however promising their start, since true faith perseveres. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers see real believers who can lose what they had. Both treat the parable as a warning to keep hearing and bearing fruit.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 4:1–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: A small clay oil lamp was the only light in a one-room house. A ‘basket’ was a measuring bowl for grain.
4.mean: Nobody lights a lamp to hide it. ‘For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed’: the kingdom, now partly hidden in parables, will one day be fully seen. Then a warning about listening: ‘With the measure you use, it will be measured to you’. ‘For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.’
4.big: Those who listen carefully receive more; those who ignore what they have heard lose even that.

4.ctx: This parable is found only in Mark.
4.mean: ‘The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground.’ He sleeps and wakes, ‘and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how. All by itself the earth produces a crop’. When the grain is ripe, he puts in the sickle, ‘because the harvest has come’ (echoing Joel 3:13).
4.big: The sower sows, but God gives the growth, quietly, steadily and beyond our understanding, until the harvest.
4.diff: Christians of every tradition find encouragement here for evangelism and patience. Wesley, typically, also stressed human effort alongside God’s: the earth brings forth no corn ‘without both the care and toil of man’. Calvin stressed that the growth is God’s alone.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Mark 4

4.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
4.ctx: The black mustard seed was proverbially the tiniest seed. The plant can grow to around three metres in a season.
4.mean: The kingdom of God ‘is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth’, but grows into ‘the largest of all garden plants’, so big that ‘the birds of the air nest in its shade’, an image the prophets used for a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12). Mark adds that Jesus taught many such parables ‘to the extent that they could understand’, and explained everything privately to his disciples.
4.big: From a Galilean teacher and twelve followers, the kingdom of God will grow beyond all expectation.
4.diff: ‘The smallest of all seeds’. Botanically, some seeds (such as orchid seeds) are smaller. Jesus is using the proverbial smallest seed known to his hearers, in the way people still speak of something as small as a mustard seed, not giving a botanical ranking.

4.ctx: The Sea of Galilee lies about 210 m below sea level, surrounded by hills. Cold air can funnel down the valleys and raise sudden violent storms.
4.mean: Crossing at evening, they are caught in a ‘violent windstorm’, and the boat is being swamped. Jesus is asleep in the stern on a cushion, fully human and exhausted. They wake him: ‘Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?’ He rebukes the wind and says to the sea, ‘Silence!’ and ‘Be still!’, and ‘it was perfectly calm.’ Then: ‘Why are you so afraid?’ … ‘Do you still have no faith?’ Now they are more afraid than before: ‘Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?’
4.big: The one asleep in the boat is the Lord who stills the sea (Psalm 107:28–29), and his presence is the answer to fear.

5.ctx: The east side of the lake was largely Gentile territory, part of the Decapolis (‘Ten Cities’). Jews regarded pigs, tombs and demons as unclean; this man was surrounded by all three.
5.mean: A man with an unclean spirit lives among the tombs, too strong to be chained, ‘crying out and cutting himself with stones’. He runs and falls before Jesus: ‘What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?’ Asked his name, he says, ‘My name is Legion,’ ‘for we are many.’ (A Roman legion was some 5,000 soldiers.) The demons beg to be sent into a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rush into the sea and drown. The townspeople come and find the man ‘sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.’ They beg Jesus to leave. The man asks to go with him, but Jesus sends him home: ‘tell them how much the Lord has done for you’. He proclaims ‘how much Jesus had done for him’ throughout the Decapolis.
5.big: No one is too far gone for Jesus; and the first missionary to the Gentile Decapolis is a man who had been possessed by a legion.
5.diff: The pigs. Readers have long asked why Jesus allowed the loss of the herd. Calvin admits ‘the reason of it is not known by us with certainty’, but suggests the demons aimed ‘to excite the inhabitants of that country to curse God on account of the loss of the swine’. He adds that the event shows demons are real spirits, not just human vices. Others note that it showed the man, visibly, that his tormentors had really gone, and that one human life is worth more than many animals.

b: Mark’s earliest manuscripts say ‘the region of the Gerasenes’; others read Gadarenes or Gergesenes (BSB footnote), and Matthew’s best manuscripts say Gadarenes (Matthew 8:28). The ancient copyists were already wrestling with the geography.

Gerasa (modern Jerash, in Jordan) was a famous city, but about 55 km from the lake, too far for the pigs to rush into the sea. Gadara (Umm Qais) was about 10 km south-east of the lake and controlled land down to the shore. Gergesa, at modern el-Kursi on the east shore, has steep slopes near the water and ancient caves that could have been tombs; Origen (3rd century) proposed it.

A common solution is that Mark and Luke name the wider district by its best-known city, and Matthew by the nearer city that owned the land; ‘region of’ is a broad term. The incident itself fits the east shore, Gentile country with pig herds, and Kursi is the site most often suggested. The exact spot cannot be fixed.

Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 5:1–20 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Gerasenes’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

5.ctx: A synagogue leader was a respected lay official. A woman with continual bleeding was ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:25) and anyone she touched became unclean, so she would have been excluded from much of normal life.
5.mean: Jairus falls at Jesus’ feet: his little daughter is dying. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years, impoverished by doctors, touches Jesus’ cloak from behind and is healed at once. Jesus stops: ‘Who touched My garments?’ She comes forward trembling and tells him everything. ‘Daughter,’ he says, ‘your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.’ He restores her publicly, not just physically. Meanwhile news comes that Jairus’s daughter is dead. Jesus says, ‘Do not be afraid; just believe.’ At the house the mourners laugh at him for saying, ‘The child is not dead, but asleep.’ He takes her hand: ‘Talitha koum!’, which means ‘Little girl, I say to you, get up!’, and she gets up and walks. He tells them to give her something to eat.
5.big: Jesus has time for the outcast and power over death; for him, death is like sleep from which he wakes people.
5.diff: ‘Your faith has healed you’. Jesus credits faith, but the power is his (verse 30), and her faith was weak and partly superstitious. Christians have always prayed for healing; they differ on how far healing should be expected today. Pentecostals such as the Assemblies of God teach that deliverance from sickness ‘is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers’, while admitting, ‘We do not understand fully why some are healed and others are not.’ Most other traditions pray for healing while accepting that God does not always grant it in this life (compare 2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The story of the twelve-year-old girl and the twelve-year illness interweave deliberately: Jesus is never too late.

src.l: Assemblies of God, ‘Divine Healing’ (position paper, quoting the Statement of Fundamental Truths, sec. 12)

6.ctx: Nazareth, Jesus’ home town, was a small village where everyone knew his family.
6.mean: Jesus teaches in his home synagogue, and the people are astonished: ‘Where did this man get these ideas?’ But astonishment turns to offence: ‘Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?’ They knew him too well to believe in him. Jesus replies, ‘Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.’ ‘So He could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them. And He was amazed at their unbelief.’
6.big: Familiarity with Jesus’ ordinary life became, for his own town, a reason not to believe.
6.diff: ‘Could not’. This does not mean Jesus’ power failed. In Mark, miracles are not shows to force belief (8:11–12); where people refuse to trust him, he does not impose them. Who were Jesus’ brothers and sisters? Christians hold three views. Most Protestants today take them as younger children of Mary and Joseph, the plainest reading of the words (the view of Helvidius in the 4th century). Orthodox tradition (following Epiphanius) holds they were Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. Catholic teaching (following Jerome) holds they were close relatives; the Catechism says James and Joseph are ‘the sons of another Mary’ (500; compare 15:40). The Reformers did not take the first view: Calvin said Helvidius ‘displayed excessive ignorance in concluding that Mary must have had many sons’, since ‘brothers’ in Hebrew usage can mean relatives; and Wesley wrote that Mary ‘as well after as before she brought Him forth, continued a pure and unspotted virgin’. The Greek word can mean relatives, but its normal sense is brothers, and Mark lists them with their mother. Nothing in the gospel depends on the answer.

b: Nazareth was a small Jewish farming village on a ridge in Lower Galilee: current estimates suggest 200–500 people in Jesus’ day. No writer before the New Testament mentions it, not even Josephus, which fits a place of no importance (compare John 1:46). Excavations under the Church of the Annunciation found silos, cisterns, tombs and simple houses.

About 6 km away stood Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital after 4 BC. The word translated ‘carpenter’ (Greek tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Building work at Sepphoris would have drawn craftsmen from the surrounding villages, and many scholars think Joseph and Jesus may have worked there, though the Gospels never mention it.

6.ctx: Travelling teachers depended on hospitality. Shaking dust off the feet was what devout Jews did on leaving Gentile land: a sign of separation.
6.mean: Jesus sends the Twelve out ‘two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits.’ They are to take ‘nothing but a staff for the journey—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts’, trusting God and their hosts. If a place will not listen, they are to ‘shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them.’ ‘So they set out and preached that the people should repent. They also drove out many demons and healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil.’
6.big: Jesus shares his mission and his authority with his followers, and sends them out dependent on God.
6.diff: Anointing with oil. Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing. Catholic and Orthodox churches see here, and in James 5:14–15, the roots of the sacrament of anointing the sick: the Catholic Catechism says it ‘is alluded to indeed by Mark, but is recommended to the faithful and promulgated by James’ (1511). Calvin saw the anointing as ‘a visible token of spiritual grace’ that went with the apostles’ gift of healing, given ‘as a temporary seal of the doctrine of the Gospel’. Many Protestant churches still anoint the sick with prayer, following James 5, without calling it a sacrament.

6.ctx: Mark tells this story in a flashback while the Twelve are away. Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he was alive.
6.mean: Herod hears about Jesus, and his guilty conscience speaks: ‘John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!’ Mark explains. Herod had married Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and John had told him, ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!’ Herodias wanted John dead, but Herod ‘feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man’, and liked to listen to him. At his birthday banquet, Herodias’s daughter dances, and Herod rashly swears to give her anything, ‘up to half my kingdom!’ Prompted by her mother she asks for ‘the head of John the Baptist on a platter’. ‘The king was consumed with sorrow’, but to save face before his guests, he gives the order. John’s disciples bury his body.
6.big: A weak man who knew what was right chose to save face; and the forerunner’s death foreshadows what awaits Jesus.

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The ‘King Herod’ of Mark 6 is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of Galilee and Perea, which he governed for 43 years. Matthew and Luke give his exact title, ‘tetrarch’; Mark uses the popular ‘king’. He rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee.

Josephus confirms the outline of Mark’s account. Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. Josephus calls that first husband Herod; Mark calls him Philip. Since several of Herod the Great’s sons were called Herod, some suggest he bore both names. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says many Jews saw the defeat as God’s punishment for his killing of ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who called the Jews to righteousness and baptism.

Josephus gives a political reason for the execution: Antipas feared John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a revolt. Mark gives the personal story. The two fit together easily. Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus, Antipas’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

6.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
6.ctx: This is the only miracle (apart from the resurrection) told in all four Gospels. A denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s pay.
6.mean: The apostles return and Jesus takes them away to rest, but the crowds get there first. ‘He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd’, and he teaches them. When it grows late, the disciples want to send people away; Jesus says, ‘You give them something to eat.’ They have ‘Five—and two fish.’ He seats the people in groups on the green grass, looks up to heaven, blesses and breaks the loaves, and gives them to the disciples to distribute. ‘They all ate and were satisfied’, and twelve baskets of leftovers are collected. ‘And there were five thousand men who had eaten the loaves.’
6.big: Jesus is the shepherd Israel lacked (Ezekiel 34), who feeds his people in the wilderness as God fed them with manna.
6.diff: Some modern writers have explained the miracle as people being moved to share food they had hidden. The Gospels give no hint of this; all four present it as a miracle of multiplication, and the disciples’ failure to understand it (6:52; 8:17–21) would make no sense otherwise. The actions ‘took…blessed…broke…gave’ anticipate the Last Supper (14:22).

6.ctx: The ‘fourth watch’ was 3–6 a.m. (BSB footnote). In the Old Testament, God alone ‘treads on the waves of the sea’ (Job 9:8).
6.mean: Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain to pray. In the night he sees them ‘straining to row, because the wind was against them’, and comes to them, ‘walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them’, language that echoes God ‘passing by’ Moses and Elijah to reveal his glory (Exodus 33:19–22; 1 Kings 19:11). They think he is a ghost. ‘Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.’ (‘It is I’ is literally ‘I am’, echoing God’s name.) He gets in and the wind stops. They are astounded, ‘for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.’
6.big: Jesus does what only God does and speaks as God speaks; yet even his closest followers were slow to understand.

6.ctx: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake, south of Capernaum. The ‘fringe’ was probably the tassel that devout Jews wore on their cloaks (Numbers 15:38–39).
6.mean: As soon as they land, people recognise Jesus and run through the region carrying the sick to wherever he is. In villages, towns and countryside they lay them in the marketplaces and beg ‘just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.’
6.big: Where people come to Jesus with their need, he does not turn them away.

7.ctx: The ‘tradition of the elders’ was an oral body of rules that Pharisees believed went back to Moses, later written down in the Mishnah. Hand-washing before meals was a ritual purity custom extended from priests to everyone, not a matter of hygiene. ‘Corban’ meant a gift dedicated to God.
7.mean: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem see Jesus’ disciples eating with unwashed hands and ask why they ignore the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers with Isaiah 29:13: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.’ ‘You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.’ His example: God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother’, but their rules let a son declare his money ‘Corban’, devoted to God, and so refuse to support his parents. ‘Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down.’
7.big: Religious rules can become a way of avoiding what God actually commands.
7.diff: Scripture and tradition. Protestants read this passage as a warning that all church traditions must be tested by Scripture, the only infallible rule (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10). Calvin drew the principle that ‘all kinds of worship invented by men are of no estimation in his sight’. Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree that merely human traditions can contradict God’s word, but distinguish them from apostolic Tradition, which hands on what the apostles received and which they hold together with Scripture as one deposit of revelation. The Catholic Catechism distinguishes that Tradition from ‘the various theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions, born in the local churches over time’ (80–83). All agree that no tradition may be used to cancel a plain command of God, as the Corban rule did.

Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

7.ctx: The food laws of Leviticus 11 marked Israel out from the nations. Whether Gentile Christians had to keep them became a burning issue in the early church (Acts 10; 15; Romans 14).
7.mean: Jesus calls the crowd: ‘Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.’ Food goes into the stomach, not the heart. Mark adds his own comment: ‘(Thus all foods are clean.)’ What defiles is what comes out of the heart: ‘evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness.’
7.big: Our real problem is not outside us but inside; and Christ’s coming ends the food laws that once marked Israel off.
7.diff: Almost all churches read Mark’s comment as declaring the Old Testament food laws fulfilled and no longer binding (compare Acts 10:15; Romans 14:14). Seventh-day Adventists hold that the distinction between clean and unclean meats still applies as a matter of health. The BSB footnote gives an alternative translation of verse 19 that applies the words to digestion, but most translations follow the reading in the text.

src.l: Seventh-day Adventist Church, 28 Fundamental Beliefs, no. 22 ‘Christian Behavior’

7.h: The Faith of the Gentile Woman
7.ctx: Tyre was a wealthy Gentile city on the coast, north-west of Galilee. Jews sometimes called Gentiles ‘dogs’; the word Jesus uses here can mean little dogs or house dogs (BSB footnote: ‘puppies’).
7.mean: Jesus goes into Gentile territory and tries to stay hidden. A Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin falls at his feet and begs him to free her daughter from a demon. ‘First let the children have their fill,’ he says. ‘For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.’ Israel comes first in God’s plan. She does not argue but takes his words and turns them: ‘Yes, Lord,’ ‘even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.’ ‘Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.’ She goes home and finds it so.
7.big: God’s blessing came to Israel first, but a Gentile mother’s humble, persistent faith shows it was always meant for the nations too.

7.ctx: The Decapolis, south-east of the lake, was again Gentile territory. Mark keeps Jesus’ Aramaic word, as at 5:41.
7.mean: People bring a deaf man who can hardly speak. Jesus takes him aside, puts his fingers in his ears, spits and touches his tongue, using touch to communicate with a man who cannot hear. He looks up to heaven, sighs, and says ‘Ephphatha!’ (‘Be opened!’). The man hears and speaks plainly. The crowd say, ‘He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!’, echoing Isaiah 35:5–6, the promise of what God would do when he came to save.
7.big: Jesus does the works Isaiah said would mark God’s coming, and he deals with each person in a way they can understand.

8.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
8.ctx: This second feeding takes place in the largely Gentile region of the Decapolis (7:31). Dalmanutha (verse 10) is otherwise unknown; it was somewhere on the western shore.
8.mean: Another large crowd has been with Jesus three days with nothing to eat. ‘I have compassion for this crowd’, he says. The disciples ask, ‘Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?’, as though the first feeding had never happened. With seven loaves and a few fish he feeds about four thousand, and seven basketfuls are left.
8.big: Jesus’ compassion and provision reach Gentiles as well as Jews.
8.diff: Some scholars think the two feedings are two versions of one event. Mark clearly regards them as two (8:19–20), with different numbers, places and words for ‘basket’. Many see significance in the settings: twelve baskets among Jews, seven among Gentiles.

src.l: ‘Magdala’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

8.ctx: A ‘sign from heaven’ meant some spectacular proof directly from God, beyond the healings they had already seen.
8.mean: Pharisees come and demand ‘a sign from heaven’, to test him. ‘Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”’ He leaves them.
8.big: Jesus does not perform on demand for people who have already decided not to believe.

8.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod
8.ctx: Leaven (yeast) works its way invisibly through a whole batch of dough; it was a common picture of a spreading corrupt influence.
8.mean: In the boat with one loaf, Jesus warns, ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.’ The disciples think he is talking about bread. He asks a string of searching questions: ‘Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts?’ He reminds them of the twelve and the seven baskets. ‘Do you still not understand?’
8.big: Unbelief can be catching; and even disciples can be slow to see what is in front of them.

8.ctx: This healing, found only in Mark, comes right after Jesus rebukes the disciples for having eyes and not seeing (8:18).
8.mean: At Bethsaida Jesus leads a blind man out of the village, spits on his eyes, lays hands on him and asks, ‘Can you see anything?’ ‘I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.’ Jesus lays hands on him again, ‘and he could see everything clearly.’
8.big: A two-stage healing, placed where Mark puts it, pictures the disciples: they see something of Jesus, but not yet clearly.
8.diff: Some ask whether the first touch ‘failed’. The Gospel does not suggest Jesus was struggling. Most commentators see an acted parable: in the next scene Peter sees that Jesus is the Christ, but blurrily, because he cannot accept a suffering Christ.

b: Bethsaida (‘house of fishing’) was the home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Josephus says that Philip the tetrarch, another son of Herod the Great, enlarged the village and renamed it Julias, in honour of the emperor Augustus’s daughter.

Two sites near the north shore of the lake are proposed. Et-Tell, about 2.5 km inland, has been excavated continuously since 1987 by Rami Arav and Richard Freund. It has impressive Iron Age remains (Arav suggests it was the capital of the Old Testament kingdom of Geshur, 2 Samuel 15:8) and a Roman-period settlement, including a building some excavators identify as a small Roman temple. Critics such as Jodi Magness say its Roman remains are too modest for the town Josephus describes. El-Araj, on the shore, was long thought to have only later remains, but excavations led by Steven Notley and Mordechai Aviam since 2016 have reported a Roman-era bathhouse (1st–3rd centuries AD) and a later Byzantine church. Arav replies that there is not yet evidence of an earlier Jewish fishing village there. Scholars are divided.

8.ctx: This is the turning point of Mark. Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, 40 km north of the lake, a city full of pagan worship.
8.mean: On the road Jesus asks, ‘Who do people say I am?’ They report the popular views: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. ‘But what about you?’ Jesus asked. ‘Who do you say I am?’ Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ.’ Jesus warns them not to tell anyone, because the word ‘Christ’ (Messiah) meant to most people a conquering king, and he must first teach them what kind of Christ he is.
8.big: Everything turns on the question every reader must answer: ‘Who do you say I am?’
8.diff: Peter and the ‘rock’. Mark, traditionally Peter’s Gospel, records only Peter’s confession. Matthew adds Jesus’ reply, ‘on this rock I will build My church’ and the keys (Matthew 16:18–19). Catholic teaching holds that the Church is ‘built on Peter’, who received ‘a unique mission’ that continues in his successors, the bishops of Rome (Catechism 552–553). Orthodox tradition honours Peter’s primacy among the apostles but does not accept the papacy’s claims of jurisdiction. Most Protestants follow Calvin in taking the rock to be Peter as confessor of Christ, or the faith he confessed, which is ‘the common foundation of the whole Church’. See the note on Matthew 16.

hist.t: Caesarea Philippi and the shrine of Pan
b: The city stood beside a large cave from which one of the sources of the Jordan flowed. In the Greek period the cave became a shrine to the god Pan, and the place was called Panias (the modern name is still Banias). About 20 BC the emperor Augustus gave the area to Herod the Great, who built a white marble temple to Augustus there, according to Josephus. Herod’s son Philip developed the town into a city and named it Caesarea in honour of the emperor, adding his own name to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast.
The cave can still be seen at Banias. Many preachers draw out the setting: among shrines to Pan and to a deified emperor, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ.

8.ctx: Nothing in popular Jewish expectation prepared people for a Messiah who would be killed. This is the first of three predictions (compare 9:31; 10:33–34).
8.mean: Now Jesus begins ‘to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again.’ ‘Must’: this is God’s plan, foretold in Scripture. He says it plainly. Peter takes him aside and rebukes him. Jesus, looking at the disciples, rebukes Peter publicly: ‘Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.’ Moments after confessing Christ rightly, Peter speaks for Satan, offering the same temptation as the wilderness: glory without the cross.
8.big: The Christ must suffer, die and rise; any version of him without the cross is the devil’s idea.

8.ctx: Mark’s first readers knew exactly what ‘take up his cross’ meant: the condemned man carried his own crossbeam to his execution. Some of them may have watched fellow believers die under Nero.
8.mean: Jesus calls the crowd as well as the disciples: ‘If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.’ The logic is the gospel’s paradox: ‘whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.’ ‘What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?’ And whoever is ashamed of Jesus now, ‘the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.’
8.big: Following a crucified Messiah means dying to self; but that is the only way to find life.

9.ctx: Moses represented the Law and Elijah the Prophets; both had met God on a mountain (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19). The cloud recalls God’s glory filling the tabernacle. The mountain is not named.
9.mean: ‘Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power.’ Six days later Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, ‘There He was transfigured before them.’ His clothes become ‘radiantly white, brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them.’ Elijah and Moses talk with him. Peter, terrified, suggests building three shelters, as if the three were equals. A cloud covers them and a voice says: ‘This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!’ Suddenly they see only Jesus. Coming down, he tells them to tell no one ‘until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.’ They ask about Elijah coming first; Jesus says Elijah has come, and ‘they have done to him whatever they wished’, meaning John the Baptist.
9.big: For a moment the disciples see the glory hidden in Jesus, and the Father tells them to listen to him, above Moses and Elijah.
9.diff: ‘Some standing here’ (verse 1). This saying puzzles readers, since the disciples died before Jesus returned. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take it to refer to the Transfiguration that immediately follows, a preview of his glory (compare 2 Peter 1:16–18). Calvin took it as the ‘manifestation of heavenly glory, which Christ began to make at his resurrection, and which he afterwards made more fully by sending the Holy Spirit’. Others think of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Each view finds a real coming of the kingdom ‘with power’ in the disciples’ lifetime.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 8:30–9:1 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Transfiguration’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

9.h: The Boy with an Evil Spirit
9.ctx: While the three were on the mountain, the other disciples had failed to help a desperate father.
9.mean: Jesus comes down to an argument. A father explains that a spirit throws his son down, makes him foam, grind his teeth and become rigid, and has often thrown him into fire and water; the disciples could not drive it out. ‘O unbelieving generation!’ Jesus says. The father pleads, ‘if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.’ ‘“If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!”’ ‘Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”’ Jesus commands the spirit out, and lifts the boy, who looks dead, to his feet. Privately the disciples ask why they failed. ‘This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.’
9.big: Jesus welcomes weak, mixed faith that turns to him; and his followers’ power depends on dependence on God in prayer.
9.diff: ‘Prayer and fasting’. Later manuscripts add ‘and fasting’ in verse 29 (BSB footnote, as in the KJV). The earliest manuscripts have ‘prayer’ only. Epilepsy? The symptoms resemble epilepsy, and Matthew uses a word often translated ‘epileptic’ (17:15). The Gospels present this case as demonic; they do not imply that epilepsy in general is.

9.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion
9.ctx: Jesus is now travelling quietly through Galilee towards Jerusalem.
9.mean: Jesus avoids the crowds ‘because He was teaching His disciples’: ‘The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.’ ‘But they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.’
9.big: Jesus kept telling them plainly; they did not want to hear.

9.ctx: In the ancient world children had no status. To welcome a child brought no honour or advantage.
9.mean: In Capernaum Jesus asks what they were arguing about on the road. Embarrassed silence: they had been arguing ‘about which of them was the greatest’, straight after he had spoken of his death. He sits down, as a teacher did, and says, ‘If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.’ He takes a child in his arms: ‘Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me’, and the Father who sent him. John reports that they tried to stop someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name ‘because he does not accompany us.’ ‘Do not stop him’, says Jesus. ‘For whoever is not against us is for us.’ Even ‘a cup of water’ given because they belong to Christ will be rewarded.
9.big: Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom is measured by service to the least important; and his people should not be jealous of others working in his name.

9.ctx: ‘Hell’ here is Gehenna (BSB footnote), the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a site of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31) and a symbol of God’s judgment. Verse 48 quotes the last verse of Isaiah (66:24).
9.mean: Anyone who causes ‘one of these little ones who believe in Me’ to stumble would be better off thrown into the sea with a millstone round his neck. Then, in deliberately shocking pictures: if your hand, foot or eye causes you to sin, cut it off or pluck it out. ‘It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go into hell, into the unquenchable fire’, ‘where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’’
9.big: Sin is so deadly that nothing is too precious to give up in order to avoid it; Jesus means the urgency, not literal self-harm.
9.diff: The nature of hell. The historic teaching of the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches is that hell is eternal, conscious punishment: the Catholic Catechism ‘affirms the existence of hell and its eternity’, its chief punishment being ‘eternal separation from God’ (1035); the Westminster Confession speaks of ‘eternal torments’ (33.2). Another view, annihilationism or conditional immortality, holds that the unrepentant are finally destroyed, so that the fire is unquenchable in its effect rather than in endless suffering. It is held by Seventh-day Adventists and some evangelicals; John Stott made what one reviewer called ‘a well-argued, yet tentative, case’ for it in 1988. Both views take Jesus’ warnings with the utmost seriousness.

9.ctx: Salt preserved food and was added to every sacrifice (Leviticus 2:13). Salt from the Dead Sea area, mixed with other minerals, could lose its taste.
9.mean: ‘For everyone will be salted with fire.’ This is one of the hardest sayings in Mark. Most take it to mean that every disciple will be tested and purified by suffering, as sacrifices were salted. ‘Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.’ The disciples who argued about greatness (9:34) need the distinctive quality that makes them useful, and peace with each other.
9.big: Disciples will be refined by trial; they must keep their distinctive savour and live at peace.

10.ctx: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 regulated divorce. Rabbis debated its grounds: the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for serious sexual misconduct; the school of Hillel for almost any reason. Herod Antipas, in whose territory Jesus now was, had divorced to remarry (6:17–18).
10.mean: Pharisees ask, to test him, ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?’ Jesus asks what Moses commanded. ‘Moses permitted a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away.’ Jesus says Moses wrote that ‘because of your hardness of heart’. He goes back further, to creation: ‘God made them male and female’, and ‘the two will become one flesh.’ ‘Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.’ In private he tells the disciples: ‘Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her. And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.’
10.big: Marriage is God’s work, joining a man and a woman as one for life; divorce is a concession to sin, not God’s design.
10.diff: Matthew’s account adds an exception, ‘except for sexual immorality’ (Matthew 19:9). Catholic teaching holds that ‘a ratified and consummated marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power or for any reason other than death’ (Catechism 2382); remarriage after civil divorce is not recognised while the first spouse lives (1650), though a marriage may be declared null if it was never valid. The Reformed confessions allow divorce and remarriage for ‘nothing but adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied’ (Westminster Confession 24.6, drawing on Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:15). The Orthodox Church, by ‘economy’ (pastoral concession), may permit a second marriage after divorce, with penitential prayers in the service. Many evangelicals hold one of these two Protestant positions; others are stricter. Wesley noted that Jesus’ words also condemn polygamy.

10.ctx: Parents brought children to rabbis to be blessed. The disciples thought Jesus had more important work.
10.mean: People bring little children for Jesus to touch, and the disciples rebuke them. Jesus is ‘indignant’, the only time Mark uses that word of him: ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.’ ‘And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.’
10.big: The kingdom is received, not earned, by the dependent and the small, and Jesus has time for children.
10.diff: Children and baptism. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptise infants, and have often appealed to this passage. Calvin called it ‘a shield against the Anabaptists’: since baptism is ‘the pledge and figure of the forgiveness of sins, and likewise of adoption by God, it ought not to be denied to infants’. Baptists and many other evangelicals reply that Jesus blessed the children but did not baptise them, and that baptism is for those who profess faith (1689 Baptist Confession 29.2). All agree that children are welcome to Jesus.

10.ctx: Wealth was widely taken as a sign of God’s blessing. The camel and the ‘eye of a needle’ are a deliberately absurd picture of the impossible.
10.mean: A man runs up, kneels and asks, ‘Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ ‘Why do you call Me good?’ Jesus replies. ‘No one is good except God alone.’ He lists commandments about how we treat others. The man has kept them all since his youth. ‘Jesus looked at him, loved him’, and said: ‘There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.’ He goes away sad, ‘because he had great wealth.’ Jesus tells the astonished disciples, ‘It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.’ ‘Who then can be saved?’ ‘With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.’ To Peter he promises that whatever is given up for him will be repaid ‘a hundredfold in the present age…along with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life.’
10.big: No one can earn eternal life; salvation is impossible for us and possible only for God, and anything we hold onto above Jesus must go.
10.diff: ‘Why do you call Me good?’ Jesus is not denying that he is good or divine. Many have read it as an invitation to think through what calling him good implies. Calvin read it more simply: ‘Thou falsely callest me a good Master, unless thou acknowledgest that I have come from God.’ Sell everything. Most traditions read this as a specific call to a man whose wealth was his idol, not a rule for every believer. Catholic and Orthodox monasticism has seen in it a call to voluntary poverty for some (the ‘evangelical counsels’). All agree that Jesus must come first.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 10:17–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion
10.ctx: Jerusalem is ‘up’ from the Jordan valley: about 1,000 m of climb from Jericho.
10.mean: On the road up to Jerusalem Jesus walks ahead; the disciples are amazed and the followers afraid. For the third time he tells the Twelve what will happen, in the most detail yet: he will be handed to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, handed to the Gentiles, who ‘will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again.’
10.big: Jesus walked towards his death with open eyes and set purpose.

10.h: The Request of James and John
10.ctx: At the right and left hand of a king sat his most powerful ministers. In the Old Testament, the ‘cup’ is often the cup of God’s wrath (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15).
10.mean: Right after the passion prediction, James and John ask for the top seats ‘in Your glory.’ ‘You do not know what you are asking,’ Jesus replies. ‘Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?’ They say they can. He says they will share his sufferings (James was later executed, Acts 12:2), but the places of honour are not his to give. The other ten are indignant. Jesus contrasts Gentile rulers who ‘lord it over them’ with his way: ‘whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant’. ‘For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.’
10.big: Jesus turns greatness upside down, and gives the key to his death: a ransom paid in his life, in place of many.
10.diff: A ransom ‘for many’. A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive; the Greek preposition means ‘in place of’. All traditions read verse 45 as a statement of Christ’s substitutionary, redeeming death; Calvin: ‘his life is the price of our redemption’. They differ over ‘many’. Reformed theology (‘definite’ or ‘particular’ redemption) holds that Christ’s death, sufficient for all, was intended to redeem effectually those the Father gave him (Canons of Dort II.3, 8). Arminian (Wesleyan) theology reads it as everyone: Wesley wrote, ‘Even for as many souls as needed such a ransom’. Catholic teaching likewise says ‘this last term is not restrictive’, and that Christ ‘died for all men without exception’ (Catechism 605).
